# Supatype: full context for language models

> Zero drift: one set of TypeScript types runs the whole stack, database to component. One schema derives the Postgres tables, migrations, row-level security, REST and GraphQL APIs, auth, storage, realtime, Studio editing views and the typed client. Self-hostable. SDKs MIT, CLI and services Apache 2.0, schema engine source-available under BSL 1.1.

This file is the expanded companion to https://www.supatype.com/llms.txt: a summary first, then the full text of every docs and guide page. Prefer linking agents here when they need product facts without scraping HTML.

## What it is

Supatype lets developers define backend data models as TypeScript `Model<>` types. That schema is the contract. From it, the platform generates and keeps in step:

- PostgreSQL tables, indexes and migrations, with a recorded rollback and a risk class for every change (safe, cautious, destructive)
- Row-level security policies from access rules on models and fields (`Public`, `LoggedIn`, `Owner<>`, `OwnerFrom<>`, `Role<>`, combined with `Any<>`, `All<>`, `Not<>`)
- REST (PostgREST) and GraphQL (pg_graphql) APIs, both running as the caller so row-level security applies
- The typed client and framework bindings your components use
- Auth (email and password, magic links, OAuth providers, MFA)
- Storage buckets from `Bucket<>` types, with accept lists, size limits, access rules, image transforms and time-limited signed URLs
- Realtime change subscriptions, presence and broadcast; each event, deletes included, reaches only subscribers allowed to read that row
- Studio: a schema-generated admin and CMS (lists, forms, rich text, blocks, media library, drafts, versions, live preview, SQL runner, migration history). Four roles on self-host: admin, developer, editor and viewer (Cloud adds owner and billing), each acting under the project's own access rules unless an owner or admin acts elevated

"Zero drift" means: change a field once and every layer follows; rename a field and the TypeScript build fails instead of production.

## What it is not

- Not a proprietary document store: data lives in standard Postgres, and a `pg_dump` takes it anywhere.
- Not "SQL first, then generate types". Types are upstream; SQL is generated.
- Not a migration tool that guesses. Renames are declared (`supatype rename`, recorded in `supatype/renames.json`); an undeclared drop is refused until you consent.

## How developers use it

1. Install the CLI (`npm install -g @supatype/cli`) and create a project with `supatype init`.
2. Author models in `schema/index.ts`.
3. Run `supatype dev`. It starts the stack in Docker Compose (or natively), applies the schema, and on every save migrates the database and regenerates the typed client. It keeps running; use a second terminal for other commands. It stops with its stack when the process that started it exits (a killed script, a cancelled CI job), as on Ctrl+C; to leave a stack running with nothing attached, use `supatype self-host compose up -d`. If `dev` itself is killed (its process ended, or its window closed before it finished stopping), the stack can be left running: the next `supatype dev` offers to stop it, and `supatype self-host compose down` stops it now.
4. Apply the schema to another database (staging, production, a self-hosted server) with `supatype push`. `supatype diff` previews a change; `supatype migrate` writes the SQL without applying it.
5. Deploy: self-host with `supatype self-host compose up` on a server you own, or Supatype Cloud (`supatype link`, `supatype deploy`), which is coming soon: join the waiting list at https://www.supatype.com/#cloud.
6. Bring an existing database: `supatype pull --out schema/index.ts` drafts the types from it; `supatype adopt` hands Supatype tables that already exist under the schema's names.

## Stack notes

- Schema engine: a Rust binary the CLI downloads from releases.supatype.com. It plans and applies migrations, policies and grants, waits at most a few seconds for table locks, and builds indexes and validates constraints online on tables with rows.
- Gateway: Kong in front of PostgREST, `supatype-server` (Go: auth and the gateway), storage, realtime and the Deno functions worker. The gateway decides CORS: the site URL, `api.corsOrigins` and a list saved in Studio; `*` only when written.
- Extensions (PostGIS, pgvector, unaccent, pgcrypto) are created in the `extensions` schema; their functions are not API endpoints, so expose one through a SQL function of your own. REST is PostgREST 14.18, which needs a JWT secret of at least 32 characters.
- Realtime: a WAL-based service (`supatype/realtime`) reading logical replication; it judges every event, deletes included, against the schema's generated read rules.
- Images: `supatype/postgres` (Postgres 17 with PostGIS, pgvector, pg_graphql and others), `supatype/server`, `supatype/realtime`, `supatype/storage`, `supatype/studio`, `supatype/functions-worker`, `supatype/schema-engine`.

## Building an app: key facts

Schema (https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html):
- Models are `Model<Fields, Meta>` types exported from `schema/index.ts`, imported from `@supatype/types`. The table name is the type name in snake case (`BlogPost` is `blog_post`); `tableName` overrides it.
- Fields are required unless wrapped in `Optional<>`. Plain `string`, `number` (float) and `boolean`, a union of string literals for an enum, and `Int`, `UUID`, `Timestamp`, `JSON<T>`, `RichText`, `Blocks<T>`, `Slug<"title">`, `ImageAsset<Bucket>`, `SupatypeAuthUserId`.
- `RelatedTo<M>` adds `<field>_id`, nullable unless `{ required: true }`, `onDelete` default `"restrict"`. `HasMany` and `HasOne` add no column. `ManyToMany` makes one junction per pair, named from both tables in alphabetical order (`post_tag`).
- Access rules per `read`, `create`, `update`, `delete`: `Public`, `LoggedIn`, `Private`, `Owner<"col">`, `OwnerFrom<"rel">`, `Role<"name">` (reads `app_metadata.role`), `Any`, `All`, `Not`, and comparisons `Eq`, `Neq`, `Gt`, `Gte`, `Lt`, `Lte`, `Like`. An operation with no rule is denied.
- Field rules go in `access.fields`; an unreadable column comes back `null`. A model with `versions` cannot have field rules.
- `versions: { drafts: true }`: the model's table holds the published record; drafts and history are in `<table>_versions`; direct API writes to the live row are refused.
- `SupatypeAuthUserId` has no foreign key unless `onDelete` (`"cascade"`, `"restrict"`, `"setNull"`) is set; with an `Owner<"col">` create rule it defaults to the caller's id.
- Renames are recorded with `supatype rename` in `supatype/renames.json`. `supatype push --yes` does not ask about renames.

Client (https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html):
- Import `createClient` from the generated `supatype/generated/client.ts`, with no type argument. It knows which models keep drafts.
- On a drafts model, `update` saves a draft; `update(data, { publish: true })` also publishes; `.draft()` reads drafts; `rpc("publish", { model_table, record_id }, { schema: "supatype" })` publishes.
- Realtime: `from(table).subscribe(cb, { event })`. Functions: `functions.invoke(name, { body })`. `error` is a plain object with `message` and `code`; auth and storage calls throw on a network failure.
- GraphQL: `graphql<T>(query, variables)`. Rich text, blocks and json fields come back as objects, not the JSON strings pg_graphql sends: the client reads the schema once per role and decodes every `JSON` scalar field the query selects, through aliases, fragments, relations and lists. A field it cannot place stays as returned.

Seeding (https://www.supatype.com/docs/seeding.html):
- `seeds/*.ts` run alphabetically, each exporting `default async function seed({ db, expr, log }: SeedContext)` from `@supatype/cli/seed`. The builder records writes; the engine applies each file in one transaction.
- Prefer `upsert({ where, data })` keyed by a primary or unique key. Nested `create` children under an upsert are added only when no identical child exists.
- `RichText` accepts a plain string. `expr.default()` (`{ "$default": true }`) resets a column to its default. Relations take `{ connect: { key: value } }`.
- Seeds cannot create sign-in users: create them with `supatype admin create-user` or the auth API, then reference their ids. Many-to-many rows go through `db.$sql`.

Studio roles (https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html):
- Self-host roles: admin, developer, editor, viewer. Only admins give or change Studio roles, and a developer cannot change an admin's account.
- Admins and developers work with full access (service role, no rules or masks). Editors and viewers work in Studio mode: the app's row rules are skipped, field rules and masks apply.
- Try it, GraphQL and Invoke offer "Send as": Me (default), Anonymous, Service role (admins and developers only), or a pasted token.
- Grant a role in Studio under Authentication > Users (Studio access), or with `supatype admin create-user --role <role>` and `supatype admin set-role`.

## Differentiators vs common alternatives

| Alternative | Typical gap vs Supatype |
|-------------|-------------------------|
| Supabase | Strong Postgres platform; types are introspected after the fact, RLS is hand-written SQL, and the Studio is a database console rather than a CMS |
| Payload CMS | Strong CMS; you assemble auth, storage, realtime and the database yourself |
| Prisma | Schema to types and migrations; you still write access rules and the API |
| Convex / Firebase | Type-safe DX; not Postgres, no SQL |

## Licensing & status

- Client SDKs, types, framework bindings, auth UI and plugins: MIT.
- CLI, Studio, storage, realtime, functions worker and the self-host control plane: Apache 2.0.
- Schema engine: source-available under the Business Source License 1.1 (SPDX `BUSL-1.1`), Licensor Supatype Ltd. Source: https://github.com/supatype/schema-engine. Production use is allowed, including commercial apps, self-hosting and agencies hosting client apps. Not allowed without a commercial licence: offering Supatype or the engine to others as a hosted or managed service (paid or free), or selling a product whose primary value is the engine. Each version becomes Apache 2.0 four years after its release. `supatype-engine licence` prints the terms; commercial licences: licensing@supatype.com.
- Each package's `LICENSE` file and `license` field are authoritative.
- Supatype is pre-1.0 and in active development; APIs and config may change between releases.

## Get started

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/

Run the stack on your machine, self-host it with Docker Compose, ship changes and upgrade Supatype components.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### Local development

Install the CLI, scaffold a project, and run the full stack on your machine. Supatype runs it in **Docker** by default. Choose **Native** during `supatype init` if you would rather use host binaries and no Docker.

#### 1. Install the CLI

```sh
$ npm install -g @supatype/cli
```

The CLI needs Node.js 22 or later. For a machine without Node, the [CLI](https://www.supatype.com/docs/cli.html#usage) page has a standalone binary. The first run downloads the binaries it needs into `~/.supatype/cache/`.

#### 2. Create a project

```sh
$ mkdir my-app && cd my-app
$ supatype init
```

`supatype init` writes `package.json`, `supatype.config.ts`, a starter schema and `public/`, installs dependencies with your package manager and writes the API keys to `.env`. Run `npm install` or `supatype keys --write` yourself only if you passed `--no-install` or `--no-keys`. Pass `-y` to take every default without being asked.

It also writes `seed.ts` and an empty `seeds/` for [seeding](https://www.supatype.com/docs/seeding.html). `package.json` lists `@supatype/cli` and `@supatype/types` as dev dependencies, because they run only at build time. The passwords and the JWT secret in `.env` are random for each project.

#### 3. Start the stack

```sh
$ supatype dev
```

`supatype dev` applies your schema when it starts, then watches it: each save migrates the database and regenerates the typed client. It keeps running, so use a second terminal for other commands. `supatype push` applies the schema to another database, such as a server you deploy to.

It stops with its stack when the process that started it exits, as it does on Ctrl+C: a script that is killed, or a cancelled CI job, leaves nothing running. To leave a stack running with nothing attached, use `supatype self-host compose up -d`.

A script that starts `dev` in the background should `exec` it, so the process ID the script holds is `dev` itself and stopping it stops the stack cleanly:

```sh
(cd my-app && exec npx supatype dev) &
DEV_PID=$!
# ... run your tests ...
kill "$DEV_PID"; wait "$DEV_PID"
```

If `dev` itself is killed (its process ended, or its window closed before it finished stopping), the stack can be left running. The next `supatype dev` finds it and offers to stop it, and `supatype self-host compose down` stops it now.

The gateway serves REST at `/rest/v1/`, auth at `/auth/v1/`, storage and realtime. With Docker it listens on `http://localhost:<gateway-port>`: init picks a free port per project and writes the URL to `.env` as `API_EXTERNAL_URL` (the port alone is `SUPATYPE_KONG_PORT`). With Native it listens on `http://localhost:54321`.

For direct SQL, Docker publishes Postgres on `127.0.0.1` at `SUPATYPE_DEV_DB_PORT` (54329 unless set), and `dev` points `DATABASE_URL` in `.env` at it. Native Postgres listens on port 5432 and checks passwords: connect as `postgres` with `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` from `.env`, or run `supatype pg psql`, which passes it for you.

#### 4. Sign in to Studio

When the stack is up, `supatype dev` prints a **Services running** panel with each address. With Docker, Studio is at `/studio/` on the gateway: `http://localhost:<gateway-port>/studio/`.

If you asked `init` for an admin, it wrote `SUPATYPE_ADMIN_EMAIL` and `SUPATYPE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` to `.env`. The first `supatype dev` or `supatype push` that finds no Studio admin creates one from them with the `admin` role, then removes the password from `.env`. Sign in with that email and password. To add one later, run `supatype admin create-user --email you@example.com`, which asks for the password.

#### 5. Know what init scaffolded

`schema/index.ts` starts with two models:

- `Profile`: one row per signed-in user, keyed by the auth user id. Any signed-in user can read profiles, and only the owner can create, update or delete theirs.
- `SiteSettings`: a singleton with a `site_name`, readable by everyone and editable by admins in Studio under Settings.

#### 6. Add a model

Add a `Post` to `schema/index.ts` and save. The running `supatype dev` migrates the database and regenerates the typed client. There is nothing to push locally.

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
import type { Model, UUID, SupatypeAuthUserId, Slug, Unique, Public, Owner } from "@supatype/types"

export type Post = Model<{
  id: UUID
  title: string
  slug: Unique<Slug<"title">>
  body: string
  author_id: SupatypeAuthUserId
}, {
  access: { read: Public; create: Owner<"author_id">; update: Owner<"author_id">; delete: Owner<"author_id"> }
}>
```

Merge the new names into the file's existing `import type` line. The table is `post`. See [Schema](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html) for field types, relations and access rules.

A change that would lose data, such as dropping a column, is never applied silently: `dev` asks first. To rename a column or table rather than drop it, see [Renames](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#renames).

#### 7. Query it

Install the client first with `npm install @supatype/client`: the generated file builds on it. Then create the client once, from the generated file, with the URL and key `init` wrote to `.env`:

`src/supatype.ts`:

```ts
import { createClient } from "../supatype/generated/client"

export const supatype = createClient({
  url: import.meta.env.VITE_SUPATYPE_URL,
  anonKey: import.meta.env.VITE_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY,
})
```

`src/posts.ts`:

```ts
import { supatype } from "./supatype"

const { data: posts, error } = await supatype.from("post").select("id, title, slug")
if (error) throw new Error(error.message)
```

The result is typed from your schema. The [Client](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html) page covers filters, writes, auth, storage and realtime.

#### Serve your frontend dev server at `/`

Keep the committed `supatype.config.ts` pointing at your production build, and proxy to Vite or Next from a gitignored `supatype.local.config.ts`:

`supatype.local.config.ts`:

```ts
// supatype.local.config.ts (your machine only)
export default {
  app: { mode: "proxy", upstream: "http://localhost:5173" },
}
```

Restart `supatype dev` after changing config. The APIs stay on their own paths.

### Self-hosting

Run the whole platform on a server you own with Docker Compose. The project layout is the same one you use locally, so the repository you develop in is the one you deploy.

#### 1. Prepare the server

Ubuntu 22.04 or similar, Docker with Compose v2, Node.js 22 or later, and the CLI:

```sh
$ npm install -g @supatype/cli
```

#### 2. Scaffold and set secrets

```sh
$ mkdir my-app && cd my-app
$ supatype init
```

`init` installs dependencies and writes generated secrets and API keys to `.env`. Set your public URLs there.

#### 3. Start Compose

```sh
$ supatype self-host compose render
$ supatype self-host compose up -d
$ supatype push
```

The gateway listens on `http://<your-host>:<gateway-port>`, the port in `SUPATYPE_KONG_PORT` in `.env` (18473 when it is unset), with Studio at `/studio/`. For HTTPS on your own domain, see step 5: the gateway serves it itself, with no reverse proxy.

> **REST BEFORE THE FIRST PUSH:** Until the first `supatype push`, every REST request answers `503` with `PGRST002`: PostgREST will not serve until the schemas it exposes exist, and the push creates them. After a push PostgREST can take up to about 30 seconds to notice, so `push` waits (at most 40 seconds) until REST answers, printing one line while it does.

> **ALLOWED ORIGINS:** Browsers may call the API from the origin of `SITE_URL` and from the origins in `api.corsOrigins` (`supatype.config.ts`) or `SUPATYPE_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` (`.env`). Any other origin is refused. Owners and admins can change the list in Studio, on the Settings page's CORS tab: a saved list is kept in the database and replaces the default until it is reset. The site URL stays allowed whatever is saved. `*` allows every origin, and only when you write it.

> **PORTS:** Only the gateway is published on every interface, at `SUPATYPE_KONG_PORT`, or on ports 80 and 443 once HTTPS is on. Postgres (`SUPATYPE_DB_PORT`, default 5432), the API server (`SUPATYPE_SERVER_PORT`, default 9999) and SeaweedFS (`SUPATYPE_SEAWEEDFS_PORT`, default 8333) bind `127.0.0.1`, so they are reachable from the server itself and nowhere else. To reach them from other machines, set `SUPATYPE_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` (or one interface's address) in `.env` and run `supatype self-host compose up -d`. Put a firewall in front first. `supatype init` lists these variables, commented out, in `.env`.

Images come from Docker Hub at `:latest`: `supatype/postgres:17-latest`, `supatype/server` (which includes realtime), `supatype/storage`, `supatype/studio`, `supatype/schema-engine`, `supatype/functions-worker` and `supatype/control-plane`. Pin versions with `SUPATYPE_*_IMAGE` in `.env` if you need to.

To run on a Postgres you already have, such as RDS or Cloud SQL, set `database: { external: { url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! } }` in `supatype.config.ts`. The stack then starts no `db` service, and every service connects there. It needs Postgres 17 or later. Field-level access rules are enforced through generated views instead of the planner rewrite in `supatype/postgres`. Realtime needs `wal_level = logical`, a free replication slot, the `wal2json` plugin and a role with `REPLICATION`. `supatype db check --connection "$DATABASE_URL"` reports what a database lacks, and `--emit` prints the SQL that fixes what it can.

Every function is handed two addresses. `ctx.url` is for calling the API from inside the function. Under Docker it is `http://kong:8000`, which no browser can open. `ctx.publicUrl` is the project's public address, `API_EXTERNAL_URL` in `.env`, for links you give to people.

Functions get no database connection by default. Setting `SUPATYPE_FUNCTIONS_DB_URL` in `.env` hands every function that URL as `ctx.dbUrl`: a raw Postgres connection as whichever role it names, which bypasses row rules and field masking. Point it at a least-privilege role granted only what your functions need, never the admin URL, for example `postgresql://functions_reader:<password>@db:5432/my-app`.

#### 4. Serve a static app

```sh
$ supatype app add --static ./public
```

This writes `app.mode: "static"` to `supatype.config.ts`. Commit it. It is a one-time step, not something to repeat on the server.

#### 5. Turn on HTTPS

Point an A record for your domain at the server and open ports 80 and 443. Then:

```sh
$ supatype add domain example.com --email you@example.com
$ supatype self-host compose up -d
```

`add domain` sets `server.mode: "standalone"`, `server.domain` and `server.tls` in `supatype.config.ts`. Commit it. On the next `compose up` the gateway listens on ports 80 and 443 instead of `SUPATYPE_KONG_PORT`, and gets and renews a Let's Encrypt certificate for the domain itself, accepting Let's Encrypt's terms under the email you gave. The app, the APIs and Studio all share the one domain.

Set `API_EXTERNAL_URL` and `SITE_URL` in `.env` to `https://example.com`: values in `.env` win over the HTTPS default. Certificates are kept in the stack's key-value store (the `valkey-data` volume, or the database when the cache is `pg_keyspace`), so they survive restarts. Port 80 also still answers plain HTTP: nothing redirects it to HTTPS.

`supatype dev` never turns HTTPS on, so the same committed config still runs on `http://localhost`.

> **RATHER NOT RUN IT YOURSELF?:** Supatype Cloud runs the same stack for you, and it is coming soon. [Join the waiting list](https://www.supatype.com/#cloud), or [book a call](https://www.supatype.com/#contact) about self-hosting with support.

### Deploy changes

Local and self-hosted environments read the same committed config. What differs between machines lives in files you do not commit.

#### Which file holds what

| File | Holds | Commit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `supatype.config.ts` | Schema path, app routing, version pins | Yes |
| `supatype.local.config.ts` | Overrides for your machine, such as the dev proxy | No |
| `supatype/renames.json` | Renames recorded with `supatype rename` | Yes |
| `.env` | `DATABASE_URL`, JWT keys, `API_EXTERNAL_URL` | No |

#### What to run when something changes

| Change | Local | Self-hosted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schema | `supatype push` | `supatype push` |
| Frontend | Nothing with the dev proxy. Otherwise `npm run build` | `npm run build`, then `compose render` and `compose up -d` |
| `supatype.config.ts` | Restart `supatype dev` | `compose render` and `compose up -d` |
| `.env` | Restart `supatype dev` | `compose up -d`, or `compose restart <service>` for one service |

> **ONE SERVICE:** `supatype self-host compose restart server` recreates just that service with the current config and `.env`. Use it rather than typing a `docker compose` command yourself: the CLI renders the compose file first, so it always names this project's folders where they are now.

#### A typical server deploy

```sh
$ cd my-app
$ git pull
$ npm install           # if package.json changed
$ supatype push         # schema migrations
$ npm run build         # static files into public/ or dist/
$ supatype self-host compose render
$ supatype self-host compose up -d
```

> **NOTE:** `supatype self-host compose up` points `DATABASE_URL` in `.env` at the Compose Postgres on `SUPATYPE_DB_PORT` (5432 unless you set it), so `push` and Studio use the same database as the stack. Leave it as it wrote it.

### Upgrading Supatype

Moving to newer Supatype components is separate from deploying your own changes, and it takes two commands, not one.

```sh
$ supatype update      # pull new images and binaries
$ supatype self-host compose up -d   # run the new images
$ supatype push        # apply the schema those components expect
```

The push is the step that is easy to miss. Grants, policies, functions and buckets are generated from your schema and only reach the database through `push`, so new images on an older database can refuse rules until it runs. The upgrade is finished after the push, not before.

> **403S AFTER AN UPGRADE:** This is the usual cause. The storage service logs the reason and names `supatype push` as the fix.

> **0.7.0:** Upgrading from 0.6.0? Deploy the new realtime image before the first push, and upgrade the CLI with the engine. The [upgrade notes](https://github.com/supatype/supatype/blob/main/UPGRADING.md) cover ownership checks, declared renames, identity columns and the rest.

### Running in production

A self-hosted stack is a Compose project, so you run it with the CLI and standard Postgres tools. Run these in the project directory on the server.

#### Health and logs

```sh
$ supatype status                          # each service and whether it is running
$ supatype self-host compose status        # Compose's own view, with health
$ supatype logs --service server --since 1h
$ supatype self-host compose logs          # every service, followed
```

`supatype logs` shows up to 100 lines per service from the past 5 minutes (`--since` changes that), then keeps following until you press Ctrl+C. Ask for a service that does not exist and it lists the ones that do. Postgres has a health check, and the services that use it wait until it passes.

> **AFTER A REBOOT:** The generated Compose file sets no restart policy except on `server`, which retries a failed start five times. Docker does not bring the stack back after the server reboots, so run `supatype self-host compose up -d` again, or from a boot-time unit of your own.

#### Backups

There is no backup command for a Compose stack. Use `pg_dump` 17 or later on the server, against `DATABASE_URL` from `.env`, which reaches the Compose Postgres on `127.0.0.1`. The dump holds every schema, including auth users, storage metadata and migration history.

```sh
$ export DATABASE_URL="$(grep '^DATABASE_URL=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)"
$ pg_dump -Fc -f backup-$(date +%F).dump "$DATABASE_URL"
$ pg_restore --clean --if-exists -d "$DATABASE_URL" backup-2026-10-28.dump
```

Stored files are not in the database. With the built-in storage they live in the `storage-data` volume, named `supatype-<project>_storage-data` in `docker volume ls`. Back that up with your usual volume tooling. `supatype self-host compose down` keeps both volumes, and only `down --volumes` deletes them.

#### Roll back a bad push

```sh
$ supatype migrations list   # what was applied, when and by whom
$ supatype rollback          # undo the last applied migration
```

`rollback` runs the reverse SQL stored with the last migration in one transaction and marks it rolled back. It then offers to restore your schema files from the snapshot stored with the migration before it, so the next push does not apply the change again. Pass `--sync-schema` to restore without asking, or `--no-sync-schema` to revert the database only. Commit the restored files.

> **DROPPED DATA:** A rollback cannot bring back a table or column the push dropped, or data a type change discarded. Restore those from a backup. Run `supatype diff` before a push to see what it will change.

## Schema

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html

Your schema is a set of TypeScript types in `schema/index.ts`. Supatype builds the tables, access rules, APIs and the typed client from it.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### Models

Each exported `Model<>` type is a table. Import the types from `@supatype/types`.

Nothing in `schema/index.ts` runs. The CLI reads it as type declarations, so a model is an `export type`, never an `export const`, and there is no builder function to call.

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
import type { Model, UUID, Optional, Public, LoggedIn } from "@supatype/types"

export type Post = Model<{
  id: UUID
  title: string
  published: boolean
  published_at: Optional<string>
}, {
  access: { read: Public; create: LoggedIn; update: LoggedIn; delete: LoggedIn }
}>
```

The table name is the type name in snake case: `Post` becomes `post`, `BlogPost` becomes `blog_post`. Set `tableName` in the second argument to choose another.

An `id: UUID` field becomes the primary key, and the database fills it in.

The second argument also takes `label` and `labelPlural` (names in Studio), `indexes`, `versions` and `singleton: true` (one row, such as site settings).

`supatype dev` applies each save. `supatype push` applies the schema to another database. `supatype diff` shows the change without applying it.

### Field types

Every field is required (`NOT NULL`) unless you wrap it in `Optional<>`. Use `Optional<>`, not `?`.

| Write | Stores |
| --- | --- |
| `string` | text |
| `number`, `Float` | a floating point number |
| `Int`, `SmallInt`, `BigInt`, `Decimal<10, 2>`, `Money` | exact numbers |
| `boolean` | true or false |
| `Timestamp`, `DateTime`, `DateOnly` | a time with zone, or a date |
| `UUID`, `Email`, `URL`, `Color`, `PhoneNumber` | text with a known format |
| `"news" \| "guide"` | an enum of those values |
| `string[]` | an array |
| `JSON<T>` | JSONB, typed as `T` in the client |
| `Vector<1536>` | a pgvector embedding with that many dimensions |
| `RichText`, `Blocks<T>`, `Slug<"title">` | content fields, see [below](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#content) |
| `ImageAsset<Bucket>`, `FileAsset` | a file in a storage bucket |
| `SupatypeAuthUserId` | the id of a sign-in user, see [below](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#owners) |

Wrap a field to add more: `Unique<T>`, `Indexed<T>`, `Default<T, value>`, `MaxLength<T, n>`, `Between<T, min, max>`.

Three wrappers shape a field in Studio. `EditorReadOnly<T>` is shown but not editable there, and the API can still write it. `Computed<T>` is filled by the database and read-only in Studio. `ComputedFrom<string, "title">` is prefilled from the fields it names on a new record, until the editor changes it.

For translated content, declare the locales once, such as `export type Locales = LocaleConfig<["en", "fr"], "en">`, and wrap a field in `Localized<T>`. It is stored as JSONB keyed by locale: `{ "en": "Hello", "fr": "Bonjour" }`. `LocalizedModel<>` localizes a model's text fields for you, and `NotLocalized<T>` opts one back out. There is no locale setting in `supatype.config.ts`.

Wrap the fields in `WithTimestamps<{ ... }>` to add `created_at` and `updated_at`, which the database fills in.

With the Native provider, `supatype dev` stores `Vector<>` and `Geo` fields as JSONB, because its Postgres has no pgvector or PostGIS. Use Docker to work with them locally.

### Relations

`RelatedTo<Model>` adds a foreign key column named after the field plus `_id`. The field `author` becomes the column `author_id`. The column can be null unless you pass `{ required: true }`.

`onDelete` takes `"cascade"`, `"setNull"`, `"restrict"` or `"noAction"`. It defaults to `"restrict"`: deleting an author with posts is refused.

`HasMany<Model>` and `HasOne<Model>` are the other side of a `RelatedTo`. They add no column. They let the client and seeds reach the related rows.

`ManyToMany<Model>` makes one junction table for the pair, whichever side declares it. It is named from both tables in alphabetical order, so posts and tags share `post_tag`. Pass `{ through: "name" }` to choose the name.

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
import type {
  Model, UUID, SupatypeAuthUserId, Timestamp, RichText, Slug, Unique, Optional, Int,
  RelatedTo, HasMany, ManyToMany, Owner, Role, LoggedIn, Public, Any, Lte, Now,
  Bucket, BucketPublic, BucketLoggedIn, BucketOwner, ImageAsset, Block, Blocks, Default,
} from "@supatype/types"

export type Author = Model<{
  id: SupatypeAuthUserId
  name: string
  bio: Optional<string>
  posts: HasMany<Post>
}, {
  access: { read: Public; create: Owner<"id">; update: Owner<"id">; delete: Owner<"id"> }
}>

export type Tag = Model<{
  id: UUID
  name: Unique<string>
}, {
  access: { read: Public; create: Role<"admin">; update: Role<"admin">; delete: Role<"admin"> }
}>

export type Post = Model<{
  id: UUID
  title: string
  slug: Unique<Slug<"title">>
  body: RichText
  sections: Optional<Blocks<HeroBlock | ProseBlock>>
  kind: "news" | "guide"
  cover: Optional<ImageAsset<Covers>>
  author: RelatedTo<Author, { required: true; onDelete: "cascade" }>
  tags: ManyToMany<Tag>
  comments: HasMany<Comment>
  views: Default<Int, 0>
  published_at: Optional<Timestamp>
}, {
  versions: { drafts: true }
  access: {
    read: Any<[Lte<"published_at", Now>, Owner<"author_id">]>
    create: Owner<"author_id">
    update: Owner<"author_id">
    delete: Any<[Owner<"author_id">, Role<"admin">]>
  }
}>

export type Comment = Model<{
  id: UUID
  post: RelatedTo<Post, { required: true; onDelete: "cascade" }>
  user_id: SupatypeAuthUserId<{ onDelete: "cascade" }>
  body: string
}, {
  access: { read: Public; create: Owner<"user_id">; update: Owner<"user_id">; delete: Owner<"user_id"> }
}>
```

The other pages use this schema in their examples. `HeroBlock`, `ProseBlock` and `Covers` are defined further down.

### Access rules

Each model has a rule for `read`, `create`, `update` and `delete`. The rules become Postgres row level security, so they hold for REST, GraphQL, realtime and the client alike.

An operation with no rule is denied. A model with no `access` at all is not reachable through the API.

| Rule | Who passes |
| --- | --- |
| `Public` | Everyone, signed in or not |
| `LoggedIn` | Any signed-in user |
| `Private` | Nobody through the API |
| `Owner<"author_id">` | The user whose id is in that column. Use `"id"`, a `SupatypeAuthUserId` field, or a relation's `_id` column |
| `OwnerFrom<"post">` | The owner of the related row, one relation deep |
| `Role<"admin">` | A user whose `app_metadata.role` is `admin` |
| `Any<[A, B]>`, `All<[A, B]>`, `Not<A>` | Either rule, both rules, or the opposite |
| `Eq`, `Neq`, `Gt`, `Gte`, `Lt`, `Lte`, `Like` | A comparison, such as `Lte<"published_at", Now>` |

In a comparison, a plain string names a column. Wrap a constant in `Literal<>`. `Now`, `AuthUid` and `Claim<"app_metadata.plan">` are also available. `IsNull<"col">` and `NotNull<"col">` test for null.

`Role<>` reads the user's `app_metadata.role`, which only the auth admin API can set. It is not the Studio role.

### Field rules and masking

A field rule limits who can read or write one column. Declare it under `access.fields`.

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
export type Profile = Model<{
  id: SupatypeAuthUserId
  display_name: string
  email: string
}, {
  access: {
    read: Public
    create: Owner<"id">
    update: Owner<"id">
    delete: Owner<"id">
    fields: { email: { read: Any<[Owner<"id">, Role<"moderator">]>; write: Owner<"id"> } }
  }
}>
```

A caller who may not read the column still gets the row, with the value masked as `null`. A write the rule refuses fails with error `42501`.

Name a relation by its column, such as `author_id`.

> **NOT WITH VERSIONS:** A model with `versions` cannot have field rules. Old versions are stored as JSON snapshots, where a column rule cannot be enforced. The schema is refused and the message asks you to drop one of the two.

### Auth user ids

`SupatypeAuthUserId` holds the id of a sign-in user. Use it for owner columns.

When the `create` rule is `Owner<"col">` and the column has no default, the column defaults to the caller's own user id. So a client can leave it out on insert.

By default there is no foreign key to the user. Deleting a user leaves their rows as they were. Add `onDelete` to get one:

| `onDelete` | When the user is deleted |
| --- | --- |
| `"cascade"` | Their rows are deleted too |
| `"restrict"` | Deleting the user is refused while they own rows |
| `"setNull"` | The column is set to null. The field must be `Optional<>` |

The push that adds the key refuses if existing rows name a user that does not exist. Its message says how many rows and how to remove them.

### Drafts and versions

`versions: { drafts: true }` keeps drafts and a history of each record. `keep` sets how many versions to keep (default 20).

The model's own table holds the published record. That is what `read` rules and the public API see. Drafts and old versions live in `post_versions`.

Publishing copies a draft into the live table. It also sets `published_at` if it is empty. The `update` rule decides who may publish.

A direct API write to the live row is refused. Save a draft with the client's `update`, then publish. See [Client](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#drafts).

`versions: { drafts: false }` keeps history only. Writes go straight to the live row.

Who sees drafts in Studio is set by `publishing.draft_visibility` in `supatype.config.ts`. The default is admin, developer and editor.

### Slugs, rich text and blocks

`Slug<"title">` fills itself from `title` when you leave it empty. While it still holds the generated value, it follows the title when the title changes. Set it yourself to keep a URL fixed. Add `Unique<>` if it must be unique.

`RichText` stores a rich text document. When you write, a plain string is accepted and becomes one paragraph. A read always returns the document.

`Blocks<T>` is a list of sections an editor arranges in Studio. Each block is `Block<"name", { fields }>`:

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
export type HeroBlock = Block<"hero", { heading: string; image: Optional<ImageAsset<Covers>> }>
export type ProseBlock = Block<"prose", { body: RichText }>
```

Each entry is stored as `{ "type": "hero", "data": { "heading": "Hi" } }`. A renderer switches on `type` and reads `data`. Rich text inside a block is not converted from a string, so write the full document there.

### Storage buckets

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
export type Covers = Bucket<"covers", {
  accessMode: "public"
  accept: ["image/png", "image/jpeg", "image/webp"]
  maxSize: "5MB"
  access: { read: BucketPublic; create: BucketLoggedIn; update: BucketOwner; delete: BucketOwner }
}>
```

A bucket has the same four rules as a model. `update` means overwriting a file. The rules are `BucketPublic`, `BucketLoggedIn`, `BucketOwner` (the uploader), `BucketRole<"name">` and `BucketPrivate`.

A rule you leave out is refused for everyone but the service role, and the push warns about it. `accessMode: "public"` serves files on a public URL whatever `read` says.

`ImageAsset<Covers>` on a model stores a reference to a file in that bucket.

### Renames

A push never guesses a rename. Renaming a field in the schema looks like a drop and an add.

In a terminal, `supatype push` asks "Was X renamed to Y?". Answer yes and it records the rename. Without a terminal it stops and prints the command to run.

```sh
$ supatype rename post.title post.headline   # a column
$ supatype rename post article               # a table
```

Renames are recorded in `supatype/renames.json`. Commit it. Every push replays it, so each database gets the same rename. `supatype rename --prune` removes entries the target database has already applied.

> **CAREFUL:** `supatype push --yes` does not ask about renames. An unrecorded rename is then pushed as a drop and an add, and the column's data is lost. Record renames first.

### What a push refuses

| Push stops when | To go on |
| --- | --- |
| A change can lose data, such as a drop | Answer yes in a terminal, or pass `--yes` in CI |
| A table the schema names exists but Supatype did not create it | `supatype adopt`, or give the model another `tableName`. The push offers to adopt in a terminal |
| Policies, grants or row level security were changed by hand | `--overwrite-drift` puts Supatype's back. To keep the hand edits, run `supatype doctor --rebaseline --accept-access-drift` |
| A versioned model has field rules | Remove one of the two |
| An `onDelete` key would point at missing users | Delete or fix those rows |

`--yes` does not override hand-edited access rules. Only `--overwrite-drift` does. Objects that Supatype did not create are never dropped or taken over.

## Client

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html

`@supatype/client` talks to your project's REST, auth, storage, realtime and functions. Its types come from your schema, so a wrong table or column fails the build.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### Create the client

Import `createClient` from the client file the CLI generates, not from `@supatype/client` directly. The generated file tells the client which models keep drafts.

`src/supatype.ts`:

```ts
import { createClient } from "../supatype/generated/client"

export const supatype = createClient({
  url: import.meta.env.VITE_SUPATYPE_URL,
  anonKey: import.meta.env.VITE_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY,
})
```

Every page in these docs imports the client from this one file. `supatype init` and `supatype keys` write `VITE_SUPATYPE_URL` and `VITE_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY` to `.env`, with `PUBLIC_` and `EXPO_PUBLIC_` copies for other frameworks. Read them rather than copying a URL from an example: `init` picks a free gateway port for each project, kept in `.env` as `API_EXTERNAL_URL`.

The session is saved and restored by default. Pass `auth: { persistSession: false }` to keep it in memory only.

`createClient` takes these options as well as `url` and `anonKey`:

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `serviceRoleKey` | Bypasses row-level security. Use it only on a server or in a trusted tool, and never ship it to a browser. |
| `headers` | Headers sent with every request. Pass a function to have it read on each request. |
| `auth.storageKey` | Key the session is saved under. Default `"supatype.auth.session"`. |
| `auth.storage` | Your own session store with `getItem`, `setItem` and `removeItem`, such as AsyncStorage in React Native. |
| `auth.cookiePrefix` | Prefix of the auth cookie `@supatype/ssr` reads. Default `"st"`. |
| `timeout`, `retry` | See [Timeouts and retries](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#timeouts-and-retries). |
| `initialSession` | A session to start with. `@supatype/ssr` uses it to hand a cookie session to the client. |
| `queryCache` | The in-memory cache for `.cache()` reads. Default: one shared cache. |

### Generated types

`supatype dev`, `supatype push` and `supatype generate` write these files. Do not edit them.

| File | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `supatype/generated/client.ts` | The `createClient` to import |
| `supatype/generated/index.d.ts` | Row, insert and update types for each table |
| `types/database.ts` | The `Database` type, for code that wants the raw shapes |

Tables are named as in the database: `post`, `comment`, `post_tag`. Calling `createClient` with no type argument picks up the generated types. To type a client against a schema you do not generate, such as a second project or a test double, pass the database type: `createClient<MyDatabase>({ ... })`.

### Read rows

`typescript`:

```ts
const { data: posts, error } = await supatype
  .from("post")
  .select("id, title, slug, author(name), comment(body)")
  .order("published_at", { ascending: false })
  .limit(10)

if (error) throw new Error(error.message)
for (const post of posts ?? []) console.log(post.title, post.author?.name)
```

`select` takes a list of columns. The result type follows the list. `*` selects every column.

Name a related table to embed it: `author(name)` follows `author_id`, and `comment(body)` lists a post's comments. A many-to-many relation embeds through its junction table: `select("title, tag(name)")`.

A to-one embed can be `null`. Write `author!inner(name)` to keep only posts that have one. Rename an embed with `writer:author(name)`.

`single()` returns one row and errors when there is not exactly one. `maybeSingle()` returns `null` for no row.

`typescript`:

```ts
const { data: post } = await supatype.from("post").select("*").eq("slug", "hello-world").maybeSingle()
console.log(post?.title)
```

### Filters

| Filter | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `eq`, `neq` | equal, not equal |
| `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte` | greater or less than |
| `like`, `ilike` | a pattern, `ilike` ignores case |
| `in` | any of a list |
| `is` | `null`, `true` or `false` |
| `not`, `or`, `match` | negation, either filter, several equalities |

`typescript`:

```ts
await supatype.from("post").select("id").in("kind", ["news", "guide"]).is("published_at", null)
await supatype.from("post").select("id").ilike("title", "%hello%").range(0, 19)
```

Reads also take `order`, `limit` and `range`. Filters work on `update` and `delete` too.

### Insert, update, delete

`typescript`:

```ts
const { data: created, error: insertError } = await supatype
  .from("post")
  .insert({ title: "Draft idea", body: "Plain text is fine.", kind: "guide", author_id: userId })
  .select("id")
  .single()
if (insertError || !created) throw new Error(insertError?.message ?? "insert failed")

await supatype.from("comment").update({ body: "Edited" }).eq("id", commentId)
await supatype.from("comment").delete().eq("id", commentId)
```

A write returns no rows unless you add `.select()`. `upsert` inserts or updates by primary key.

A `RichText` field takes a plain string on write. Owner columns with an `Owner<>` create rule can be left out: they default to the caller.

### Drafts and publishing

On a model with `versions: { drafts: true }`, `update` saves a draft. The live row does not change until the record is published.

`typescript`:

```ts
// Save a draft
await supatype.from("post").update({ title: "Better title" }).eq("id", postId)

// Save and publish in one call
await supatype.from("post").update({ title: "Final title" }, { publish: true }).eq("id", postId)

// Read drafts
const { data: drafts } = await supatype.from("post").draft().select("id, title").eq("id", postId)

// Publish the saved draft
await supatype.rpc("publish", { model_table: "post", record_id: postId }, { schema: "supatype" })
```

`insert` on a drafts model creates a draft record. Publish it to make it live. A plain `select()` reads the live table, which holds the published values.

`{ publish: true }` is only accepted on drafts models, and only when the client comes from the generated file.

### Auth

`typescript`:

```ts
await supatype.auth.signUp({ email: "alex@example.com", password: "a-long-password" })

const { data, error: signInError } = await supatype.auth.signInWithPassword({
  email: "alex@example.com",
  password: "a-long-password",
})
if (signInError) throw new Error(signInError.message)
console.log(data.session?.user.id)

const { data: { session } } = await supatype.auth.getSession()
console.log(session?.accessToken)

const { data: { subscription } } = supatype.auth.onAuthStateChange((event, current) => {
  console.log(event, current?.user.email)
})
subscription.unsubscribe()

await supatype.auth.signOut()
```

Once signed in, every request carries the user's token, so access rules see them. `onAuthStateChange` calls back at once with the current state, then on each change.

`getUser()` fetches the user from the server. Magic links, OAuth, one-time codes and MFA are on `supatype.auth` too.

### Storage

`typescript`:

```ts
const bucket = supatype.storage.from("covers")

const { data: upload, error: uploadError } = await bucket.upload(`${userId}/cover.png`, file, {
  contentType: "image/png",
  upsert: true,
})
if (uploadError || !upload) throw new Error(uploadError?.message ?? "upload failed")

const { data: { publicUrl } } = bucket.getPublicUrl(upload.path)
const { data: signed } = await bucket.createSignedUrl(upload.path, 60)
console.log(publicUrl, signed?.signedUrl)
```

`getPublicUrl` works for public buckets. `createSignedUrl` gives a link that expires after the number of seconds you pass. `download`, `list` and `remove` are on the bucket too.

The bucket's access rules from the schema decide who may upload, overwrite and delete.

### Realtime

`typescript`:

```ts
const sub = supatype.from("comment").subscribe((change) => {
  console.log(change.eventType, change.new, change.old)
}, { event: "INSERT" })

sub.unsubscribe()
```

Each change reaches only subscribers allowed to read that row. `event` is `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `*`. For broadcast and presence, use `supatype.realtime.channel(name)`.

### Functions

`typescript`:

```ts
const { data: reply, error: fnError } = await supatype.functions.invoke("hello", { body: { name: "Alex" } })
if (fnError) console.error(fnError.code, fnError.message)
console.log(reply)
```

The call goes to `/functions/v1/hello` with the user's token. A JSON response is parsed. Function names and bodies are not typed. `invoke` also takes `method` (default `POST`), `headers` and `idempotent`.

`supatype.rpc(name, params, options)` calls a Postgres function. Its options are `count`, `head`, `schema` for a function outside the default schema, and `idempotent`.

### GraphQL

`typescript`:

```ts
import type { TableRow } from "../supatype/generated/client"

type Post = TableRow<"post">
type PostPage = { postCollection: { edges: { node: Pick<Post, "title" | "body"> }[] } }

const { data, error } = await supatype.graphql<PostPage>(`{
  postCollection(first: 10) { edges { node { title body } } }
}`)
const firstParagraph = data?.postCollection.edges[0]?.node.body.root.children?.[0]
```

The query goes to `/graphql/v1` as the signed-in user, under the same access rules as REST. Pass variables as the second argument, and `{ idempotent: true }` as the third to retry a read on a transient failure.

Rich text, blocks and json fields come back as objects and arrays, not strings. pg_graphql types every json and jsonb column with its `JSON` scalar and sends it as a JSON-encoded string, so the client reads the schema once per role, finds each field of that type in your query, and decodes it. Aliases, named and inline fragments, nested relations and lists all decode. A field the client cannot place stays exactly as returned: one added since the schema was read (it reads the schema again on the next call), a document with more than one operation, or a schema it could not read.

The type argument names the answer's shape and is not checked at runtime. Build it from the generated `TableRow` types so `body` is typed as the rich text document it now is. Variables you send are not encoded: a json argument still takes a string.

Using another GraphQL client? `readGraphqlSchema` reads the `data` of an introspection answer to `GRAPHQL_SCHEMA_QUERY`, and `decodeGraphqlJsonFields(query, data, schema)` decodes an answer the same way.

### Errors

Queries, `rpc`, `functions.invoke`, auth and most storage calls return `{ data, error }`. Check `error` before using `data`.

`error` is a plain object with `message` and, when known, `code`, `status`, `details` and `hint`. Do not test it with `instanceof`. When a field validator refused the write, `field` names the column, so you can mark that input.

An insert an access rule refuses returns code `42501`. An update or delete that the rules hide matches no rows and returns no error. `single()` with no row returns `PGRST116`.

> **NETWORK FAILURES:** A network failure on a query, `rpc` or function call comes back as `error` with a code: `NETWORK_TIMEOUT`, `NETWORK_CONNECTION_REFUSED`, `NETWORK_DNS_FAILURE` or `NETWORK_ERROR`. A read still answered 429 after its last retry has code `RATE_LIMITED`. Most auth and storage calls throw instead, so wrap them in `try` when the network may fail. Three return the failure as `error` like a query: `storage.listBuckets`, `storage.createBucket` and `auth.refreshSession`. `auth.signOut` ignores a network failure and clears the session on this device anyway.

### Timeouts and retries

Every HTTP request the client makes (tables, `rpc`, `graphql`, `functions`, auth and storage, uploads included) is aborted after `timeout` milliseconds, 30000 by default. Raise it for large uploads on slow links. The realtime socket is not an HTTP request and is not covered.

Only requests that are safe to send twice are retried:

- `GET` and `HEAD` requests: table selects, storage downloads, `auth.getUser()`, and an `rpc` call with `head: true`.
- The two reads storage sends as `POST`: `list` and `createSignedUrl`.
- An `rpc`, `graphql` or `functions.invoke` call you pass `idempotent: true`.

Inserts, updates, upserts, deletes, uploads, sign-in and sign-up, and any `rpc`, `graphql` or function call without `idempotent: true` are sent once: a write that failed in flight may already have been applied, and sending it again could apply it twice. A 429 on one of these comes back as the server's own error.

A retried request is retried up to 3 times, after 200 ms, 1 s and 3 s, on a dropped connection or a 5xx. A 429 waits for its `Retry-After` (5 seconds when the header is absent). A timeout and a 4xx are never retried. `retry: false` turns retries off for every request.

`typescript`:

```ts
const { data, error } = await supatype.rpc(
  "search_posts",
  { query: "supatype" },
  { idempotent: true }, // the function only reads, so a retry is harmless
)
```

## Frameworks

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/frameworks.html

Supatype has bindings for React, Vue, Svelte and Solid, a React Native helper, and a server helper for Next.js. Each one wraps the client you already create, so everything on the [Client](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html) page still applies.

### Packages

| Package | Exports |
| --- | --- |
| `@supatype/react` | `SupatypeProvider`, `useSupatype`, `useQuery`, `useMutation`, `useFunction`, `useAuth`, `useSubscription`, `useLivePreview`, `RichText` |
| `@supatype/vue` | `supatypePlugin`, `useSupatype`, `useQuery`, `useMutation`, `useFunction`, `useAuth`, `useSubscription` |
| `@supatype/svelte` | `setSupatypeClient`, `getSupatypeClient`, `createQuery`, `createMutation`, `createFunction`, `createAuth`, `createSubscription` |
| `@supatype/solid` | `SupatypeContext`, `useSupatype`, `createQuery`, `createMutation`, `createFunction`, `createAuth`, `createSubscription` |
| `@supatype/react-native` | `createNativeClient`, `secureStoreAdapter`, `asyncStorageAdapter`, `openOAuth`, `createAuthUrlListener` |
| `@supatype/ssr` | `createServerClient` |

Every example below imports the client from `src/supatype.ts`, created once as shown in [Client: Create the client](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#setup). With Vite, read the values `supatype keys` writes to `.env`:

`src/supatype.ts`:

```ts
import { createClient } from "../supatype/generated/client"

export const supatype = createClient({
  url: import.meta.env.VITE_SUPATYPE_URL,
  anonKey: import.meta.env.VITE_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY,
})
```

Sign-in screens are covered on [Auth: Pre-built UI](https://www.supatype.com/docs/auth.html#ui), and the subscription hooks on [Realtime: Framework hooks](https://www.supatype.com/docs/realtime.html#hooks). This page does not repeat them.

### React

Wrap your app in `SupatypeProvider` and pass the client. Every hook reads the client from it and throws when there is no provider above it.

`src/Posts.tsx`:

```tsx
import { SupatypeProvider, useQuery, useMutation, useFunction } from "@supatype/react"
import { supatype } from "./supatype"

function Posts() {
  const { data: posts, loading, error, refetch } = useQuery("post", {
    select: "id, title, slug",
    order: { column: "title" },
    limit: 20,
  })
  const { mutate: removePost } = useMutation("post", "delete")
  const { invoke: greet, data: reply } = useFunction<{ greeting: string }>("greet")

  if (loading) return <p>Loading</p>
  if (error) return <p>{error.message}</p>
  return (
    <ul>
      {posts?.map((post) => (
        <li key={post.id}>
          {post.title}
          <button onClick={async () => { await removePost(undefined, { filter: { id: post.id } }); refetch() }}>Delete</button>
        </li>
      ))}
      <button onClick={() => greet({ name: "Alex" })}>{reply?.greeting ?? "Say hello"}</button>
    </ul>
  )
}

export function App() {
  return <SupatypeProvider client={supatype}><Posts /></SupatypeProvider>
}
```

#### useQuery

`useQuery(table, options)` returns `data`, `error`, `count`, `loading` and `refetch`. It runs again when the options change, and when a different user signs in or out.

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `select` | The select expression. Default `*`. |
| `filter` | Equality filters, one per column. |
| `order` | `{ column, ascending }`. Ascending by default. |
| `limit`, `offset` | Paging. `offset` only applies when `limit` is set. |
| `enabled` | `false` skips the query. |
| `refetchInterval` | Runs the query again every so many milliseconds. |
| `cache` | The same cache options as the client's `.cache()`. |
| `draft` | Reads saved drafts instead of published rows, on a model with drafts. See [Drafts and publishing](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#drafts). |

For anything `filter` cannot say, such as ranges or embeds with conditions, use the client directly through `useSupatype()`.

#### useMutation and useFunction

`useMutation(table, operation)` takes `"insert"`, `"update"`, `"delete"` or `"upsert"` and returns `mutate`, `loading` and `error`. `mutate(data, { filter, publish })` takes the rows to write; `filter` picks the rows for an update or delete, and `publish: true` publishes the drafts an update saves. It does not ask for the written rows back, so call `refetch` on your query afterwards.

`mutate` resolves with `{ data, error, count }`. There are no `onMutate`, `onSuccess` or `onError` callbacks, so an optimistic update and its rollback are yours to write.

`useFunction(name)` returns `invoke`, `data`, `error` and `loading`. `invoke(body, { method, headers })` calls `supatype.functions.invoke`. See [Functions: Call a function](https://www.supatype.com/docs/functions.html#call).

`useAuth()` returns `user`, `session`, `loading`, `error`, `signUp`, `signIn` (email and password), `signInWithOAuth`, `signInWithOtp` and `signOut`, and re-renders when the session changes. For anything else, such as MFA or a password reset, call `useSupatype().auth`. See [Auth](https://www.supatype.com/docs/auth.html).

#### Live preview

Studio can show your app in a pane beside the edit form and stream the unsaved values into it as the editor types. Tell Studio where a record's page lives in `supatype.config.ts`:

`supatype.config.ts`:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  // ...
  admin: { livePreview: { Post: { urlPattern: "https://example.com/preview/{slug}" } } },
})
```

A path such as `"/preview/{slug}"` is enough when the same deployment serves your app (`app.mode` set to `static` or `proxy`). With `app.mode: "none"`, `supatype push` refuses a path and wants the full URL.

On that page, `useLivePreview` returns the live values while Studio is sending them and your own data otherwise:

`src/PostPreview.tsx`:

```tsx
import { useLivePreview, RichText } from "@supatype/react"
import type { TableRow } from "@supatype/client"

export function PostPreview({ post }: { post: TableRow<"post"> }) {
  const { data, isPreview } = useLivePreview({ initialData: post })
  return (
    <article>
      {isPreview && <p>Preview</p>}
      <h1>{data.title}</h1>
      <RichText content={data.body} />
    </article>
  )
}
```

A message is applied only when it comes from the window framing the page, at a Studio origin. By default that is the origin of the provider's client URL, since Studio is served at `/studio/` on your API. If Studio is served somewhere else, or the page has no provider, pass `studioOrigin` with one URL or a list. Messages from any other origin are ignored with a console warning. `model` limits the hook to messages for one model.

This is the unsaved form state. To show the last saved draft instead, use `useQuery` with `draft: true`.

#### RichText

`RichText` renders a saved rich text field as React elements. Text is rendered as text, never as HTML, and links keep only a safe `href`. It works in Server Components and Client Components. Props are `content`, `className`, and `as` to choose the wrapper: `div` (the default), `article`, `section`, `aside` or `main`. A `null` content renders nothing.

### Vue

Install the plugin with your client. The composables must be called inside `setup`.

`src/main.ts`:

```ts
import { createApp } from "vue"
import { supatypePlugin } from "@supatype/vue"
import { supatype } from "./supatype"
import App from "./App.vue"

createApp(App).use(supatypePlugin, supatype).mount("#app")
```

`src/Posts.vue`:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useQuery, useMutation } from "@supatype/vue"

const { data: posts, loading, refetch } = useQuery("post", { columns: "id, title", limit: 20 })
const { mutate: removePost } = useMutation("post", "delete")

async function remove(id: string) {
  await removePost(undefined, { filter: { id } })
  await refetch()
}
</script>

<template>
  <p v-if="loading">Loading</p>
  <ul v-else>
    <li v-for="post in posts" :key="post.id">
      {{ post.title }} <button @click="remove(post.id)">Delete</button>
    </li>
  </ul>
</template>
```

Results are refs. The query runs when the component mounts. `enabled` may be a ref; the query runs again when it turns `true`. `useFunction(name)` returns `invoke(body)`, `data`, `error` and `loading`.

### Svelte

Set the client once in a parent component. The `create*` functions read it from context, so call them during component setup, then read the stores with `$`.

`src/App.svelte`:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  import { setSupatypeClient } from "@supatype/svelte"
  import { supatype } from "./supatype"
  import Posts from "./Posts.svelte"

  setSupatypeClient(supatype)
</script>

<Posts />
```

`src/Posts.svelte`:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  import { createQuery } from "@supatype/svelte"

  const { data: posts, loading } = createQuery("post", { columns: "id, title", limit: 20 })
</script>

{#if $loading}
  <p>Loading</p>
{:else}
  <ul>{#each $posts ?? [] as post (post.id)}<li>{post.title}</li>{/each}</ul>
{/if}
```

`createQuery` fetches as soon as it is created and returns readable stores plus `refetch`. `createMutation` and `createFunction` work like the Vue versions.

### Solid

Provide the client with `SupatypeContext.Provider`. Results are accessors, so call them to read.

`src/App.tsx`:

```tsx
import { For, Show } from "solid-js"
import { SupatypeContext, createQuery } from "@supatype/solid"
import { supatype } from "./supatype"

function Posts() {
  const { data: posts, loading } = createQuery("post", { columns: "id, title", limit: 20 })
  return (
    <Show when={!loading()} fallback={<p>Loading</p>}>
      <ul><For each={posts() ?? []}>{(post) => <li>{post.title}</li>}</For></ul>
    </Show>
  )
}

export function App() {
  return <SupatypeContext.Provider value={supatype}><Posts /></SupatypeContext.Provider>
}
```

The query runs on mount. `createMutation` and `createFunction` work like the Vue versions.

#### How Vue, Svelte and Solid differ from React

- The query option is `columns`, not `select`. `refetchInterval`, `cache` and `draft` are React only.
- `mutate` takes `filter` but not `publish`.
- `invoke` takes a body only, so the call is always a `POST`.
- `signIn` and `signUp` take `(email, password)` rather than an object, `signInWithOAuth(provider)` sends the browser to the provider, and there is a `resetPassword(email)`.
- There is no live preview hook or rich text component.

All four bindings run the query again when a different user signs in or out.

### React Native

`createNativeClient` is `createClient` with session storage that survives app restarts. Pass `expo-secure-store` (recommended) or AsyncStorage; without either it throws. Use the `EXPO_PUBLIC_` values `supatype keys` writes.

`src/supatype.ts`:

```ts
import * as SecureStore from "expo-secure-store"
import * as Linking from "expo-linking"
import { createNativeClient, createAuthUrlListener } from "@supatype/react-native"

export const supatype = createNativeClient({
  url: process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_URL!,
  anonKey: process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY!,
  secureStore: SecureStore,
})

// Finish sign-ins that come back through a deep link, on cold and warm start.
export const stopAuthLinks = createAuthUrlListener(supatype, { linking: Linking, pathIncludes: "auth/callback" })
```

Wrap the app in `SupatypeProvider` from `@supatype/react` and use the same hooks as on the web. The native client does not read sessions from a URL by itself, which is why the listener is there.

`openOAuth(client, { provider, redirectTo, webBrowser })` runs an OAuth sign-in in `expo-web-browser` with PKCE and returns the session, or `cancelled: true` when the user closes the browser. The ready-made native screens are on [Auth: Pre-built UI](https://www.supatype.com/docs/auth.html#ui).

### Next.js server code

In the browser the client copies the session into a cookie named `st-auth-token` (path `/`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Secure` on HTTPS). `createServerClient` from `@supatype/ssr` reads that cookie on the server and builds a client signed in as the same user. Use it in Server Components, Route Handlers and middleware.

`src/supatype-server.ts`:

```ts
import { cookies } from "next/headers"
import { createServerClient } from "@supatype/ssr"

export async function serverClient() {
  const store = await cookies()
  return createServerClient(process.env.PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_URL!, process.env.PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY!, {
    cookies: { getAll: () => store.getAll(), setAll: () => {} },
  })
}
```

`app/posts/page.tsx`:

```tsx
import { RichText } from "@supatype/react"
import { serverClient } from "@/supatype-server"

export default async function Page() {
  const supatype = await serverClient()
  const { data: posts } = await supatype.from("post").select("id, title, body")
  return posts?.map((post) => <RichText key={post.id} content={post.body} as="article" />)
}
```

A Route Handler uses `serverClient()` the same way. In middleware, read the cookies from the request and check the user with the auth server:

`middleware.ts`:

```ts
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from "next/server"
import { createServerClient } from "@supatype/ssr"

export async function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  const supatype = createServerClient(process.env.PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_URL!, process.env.PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY!, {
    cookies: { getAll: () => request.cookies.getAll(), setAll: () => {} },
  })
  const { data } = await supatype.auth.getUser()
  if (!data.user) return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/sign-in", request.url))
  return NextResponse.next()
}

export const config = { matcher: ["/account/:path*"] }
```

What the cookie handling does and does not do:

- It only reads. The `cookies` option needs both `getAll` and `setAll`, but `createServerClient` never calls `setAll`, so a no-op is fine. The browser client keeps the cookie fresh.
- A cookie whose access token has expired is ignored, and the server client runs as an anonymous caller. A page rendered after a long idle shows the signed-out view until the browser refreshes the session.
- The cookie is decoded, not verified. Queries made with it are checked by the API, so access rules hold. But do not trust `auth.getSession()` on the server to decide who someone is: call `auth.getUser()`, which asks the auth server, as the middleware above does.
- Decoding the cookie uses Node's `Buffer`. Where `Buffer` is missing, every cookie reads as expired, so run middleware on the Node.js runtime.
- Set `cookiePrefix` on both sides if you change the client's `auth.cookiePrefix`. The default is `st`.
- The server client is built from `@supatype/client`, not your generated client file, so `update(..., { publish: true })` is not accepted on it.

The browser half of a Next.js app needs the URL and anon key in `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables. `supatype keys` does not write those names, so copy the values across. Server code can read `PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_URL` and `PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY` directly.

## Auth

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/auth.html

Auth is built into the Supatype server. It signs users in, issues the tokens every request carries, and those tokens are what your schema's access rules check.

### How it runs

The auth service is part of `supatype-server`, the same process that serves REST, GraphQL, storage and functions. It answers under `/auth/v1` on your project's API URL. It keeps its users, identities and sessions in the `auth` schema of your project's database and runs its own migrations when the server starts.

- `supatype dev` with `database.provider: "docker"` (what `supatype init` writes): the server runs in the Compose stack behind Kong. Your API URL is `API_EXTERNAL_URL` in the project's `.env`.
- `supatype dev` with `database.provider: "native"`: the server runs as a local process on `server.port`, `54321` by default.
- Self-host: `supatype self-host compose up` runs the same server image. It needs `JWT_SECRET` in `.env` and fills in a blank `ANON_KEY` or `SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` from it. See [Self-hosting](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#self-host).

In local dev, sign-ups are confirmed automatically, so a new user gets a session straight away with no email round trip.

> **NOTE:** Who may open Studio, and what they may do there, is decided by Studio roles. See [Studio roles](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html).

### Sign-in methods

Each method below is a call on `supatype.auth`. The [client page](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#auth) shows the common ones in use.

| Method | Client call | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Email and password | `signUp`, `signInWithPassword` | On |
| Magic link or email code | `signInWithOtp({ email })`, then `verifyOtp` for a code | On, needs a mail provider to deliver |
| Phone code (SMS, or WhatsApp with Twilio) | `signInWithOtp({ phone })`, `verifyOtp` | Off, needs an SMS provider |
| OAuth | `signInWithOAuth({ provider })` | Off until a provider is configured |
| Provider ID token (native Apple or Google sign-in) | `signInWithIdToken` | Off until the provider is configured |
| Anonymous | `signInAnonymously` | Off |

Password reset is `resetPasswordForEmail`, and `updateUser` changes the email, password or user metadata of the signed-in user. Passwords must be at least 6 characters unless you raise `SUPATYPE_PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH`.

`signUp` takes `options.data` for user metadata, which comes back on `user.userMetadata`.

`signInWithOtp` creates the user when they do not exist, unless you pass `options.createUser: false`. For a phone, pass `phone` and optionally `options.channel` (`"sms"` or `"whatsapp"`), then call `verifyOtp` with `type: "sms"`. `resend({ type, email })` or `resend({ type, phone })` sends a confirmation or code again, where `type` is `"signup"`, `"sms"`, `"email_change"` or `"phone_change"`.

For a password reset, wait for `initialize()` on the page the link opens, then call `updateUser({ password })`. A recovery link, or `verifyOtp` with `type: "recovery"`, emits `PASSWORD_RECOVERY` once the session exists.

#### Auth errors

Auth calls put the auth server's code in `error.code`, beside `message` and `status`. Branch on the code, not the message: `invalid_credentials`, `email_not_confirmed`, `weak_password`, `user_already_exists`, `email_exists`, and `otp_expired` for an expired link. `error.code` is absent only when the answer carried none, such as a gateway's HTML error page.

#### Multi-factor

`supatype.auth.mfa` has `enroll`, `challenge`, `verify`, `challengeAndVerify` and `unenroll`. TOTP authenticator apps are on by default. Phone factors are off by default and need an SMS provider.

`enroll({ factorType: "totp" })` returns the factor's `id` and a QR code (`totp.qrCode`) and URI (`totp.uri`) to show the user. `challengeAndVerify({ factorId, code })` is `challenge` then `verify` in one call. Call the two separately when the code arrives later, as an SMS does. A verify raises the session to AAL2 and emits `MFA_CHALLENGE_VERIFIED`. `listFactors()` returns every factor in `all` and the verified ones in `totp` and `phone`. `getAuthenticatorAssuranceLevel()` reports the current and next level.

#### Anonymous users

An anonymous sign-in creates a real user with a user id and a session. Turn it on with `SUPATYPE_EXTERNAL_ANONYMOUS_USERS_ENABLED=true`. Because the user has an id, an anonymous user passes `LoggedIn` and can own rows. The token carries `is_anonymous: true`.

`signInAnonymously({ options: { data, captchaToken } })` takes optional metadata and a captcha token, and the user comes back with `isAnonymous: true`.

### OAuth providers

Each provider is switched on with environment variables named after it. For GitHub:

`.env`:

```ini
# Replace http://localhost:54321 with your API URL (API_EXTERNAL_URL)
SUPATYPE_EXTERNAL_GITHUB_ENABLED=true
SUPATYPE_EXTERNAL_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
SUPATYPE_EXTERNAL_GITHUB_SECRET=your-client-secret
SUPATYPE_EXTERNAL_GITHUB_REDIRECT_URI=http://localhost:54321/auth/v1/callback
```

The redirect URI is the auth service's callback: `/auth/v1/callback` on your API URL. Register the same URL with the provider. A provider with no client id, secret or redirect URI is refused when someone tries to use it.

Supported provider names: `apple`, `azure`, `bitbucket`, `discord`, `facebook`, `figma`, `fly`, `github`, `gitlab`, `google`, `kakao`, `keycloak`, `linkedin_oidc`, `notion`, `slack_oidc`, `snapchat`, `spotify`, `twitch`, `twitter`, `x`, `workos` and `zoom`. The auth server also accepts `vercel_marketplace`, and the older `linkedin` and `slack`, which the `_oidc` versions replace. Upper-case the name for the variable, so `linkedin_oidc` becomes `SUPATYPE_EXTERNAL_LINKEDIN_OIDC_ENABLED`.

#### The sign-in round trip

`typescript`:

```ts
const { data, error } = await supatype.auth.signInWithOAuth({
  provider: "github",
  options: { redirectTo: "http://localhost:5173/auth/callback" },
})
if (error) throw new Error(error.message)
window.location.assign(data.url)

// On /auth/callback
// The client finishes the sign-in in the URL when it starts; initialize() waits for that.
const { error: callbackError } = await supatype.auth.initialize()
if (callbackError) console.error(callbackError.message)
```

`signInWithOAuth` returns the URL; it does not navigate for you. `redirectTo` must be on the same host as `SITE_URL`, a loopback address, or match an entry in `SUPATYPE_URI_ALLOW_LIST` (comma-separated, globs allowed). Anything else sends the user to `SITE_URL` instead. An app on another domain, or a mobile deep link, needs an allow list entry.

The web default is the implicit flow, which returns tokens in the URL fragment. Pass `flowType: "pkce"` in the options for a code exchange instead; mobile apps should always use PKCE. The client finishes either from the URL when it starts, and removes the tokens from the address bar; `initialize()` resolves once it has, with any `error` the provider sent back. Do not call `getSessionFromUrl` as well: the URL no longer carries the tokens by then, so it answers with an error.

`exchangeCodeForSession(code)` does the PKCE exchange on its own. `options.scopes` asks the provider for extra scopes.

### Sessions and tokens

A session is a short-lived access token and a refresh token.

- The access token is a JWT signed with `JWT_SECRET`, valid for one hour. The client sends it as `Authorization: Bearer` on every request.
- The client refreshes it about a minute before it expires, and again on load if a saved session has already expired. If the refresh fails, the session is cleared rather than kept with a dead token.
- Refresh tokens rotate: each refresh issues a new one.
- `signOut` takes no arguments. It ends every session the user has on the server, not just this device's, and clears it locally.

In the browser the session is saved to `localStorage` under `supatype.auth.session` and mirrored to a cookie named `st-auth-token`, which `@supatype/ssr` reads on the server. Set `auth: { persistSession: false }`, `storageKey` or `cookiePrefix` on `createClient` to change this. On React Native, `createNativeClient` from `@supatype/react-native` stores the session in `expo-secure-store` or AsyncStorage.

#### Auth events

`onAuthStateChange` calls back at once with `SIGNED_IN` or `SIGNED_OUT`, then on each of these:

| Event | When |
| --- | --- |
| `SIGNED_IN` | A session starts while signed out |
| `SIGNED_OUT` | The session is cleared |
| `TOKEN_REFRESHED` | The session is replaced while signed in |
| `USER_UPDATED` | `updateUser` succeeded. The session passed to the callback carries the updated user |
| `PASSWORD_RECOVERY` | A password reset link or code produced a session, after its `SIGNED_IN` |
| `MFA_CHALLENGE_VERIFIED` | An MFA verify raised the session to AAL2 |

#### What the token says

| Claim | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `sub` | The user id |
| `role` | The database role the API runs the request as: `authenticated` for a signed-in user |
| `email`, `phone` | The user's contact details |
| `app_metadata` | Set only through the admin API. Holds the application role that `Role<>` checks |
| `user_metadata` | Set by the user, for example through `signUp` options or `updateUser`. Never trust it for access |
| `aal`, `amr` | Assurance level and how the user signed in, for MFA |
| `session_id`, `is_anonymous` | The session, and whether the user signed in anonymously |

Requests made with only the anon key have no user. Requests made with the service role key pass every access rule; keep that key on the server.

### Access rules

The access rules you declare in the schema compile to Postgres row level security that reads the verified token. Every request runs with the token's claims available to the database, so the same rule holds for REST, GraphQL and realtime. The rules themselves are listed on the [schema page](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#access).

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
import type { Model, UUID, SupatypeAuthUserId, Public, LoggedIn, Owner } from "@supatype/types"

export type Profile = Model<{
  id: SupatypeAuthUserId
  display_name: string
}, {
  access: { read: Public; create: Owner<"id">; update: Owner<"id">; delete: Owner<"id"> }
}>

export type Bookmark = Model<{
  id: UUID
  owner_id: SupatypeAuthUserId
  post_id: UUID
}, {
  access: { read: Owner<"owner_id">; create: LoggedIn; update: Owner<"owner_id">; delete: Owner<"owner_id"> }
}>
```

A profile keyed on the user id lets each user write only their own row. Bookmarks are private to whoever saved them.

#### What the rules become

The engine installs a small set of SQL functions in the `auth` schema, and every policy calls them:

| Rule or function | SQL |
| --- | --- |
| `auth.uid()` | The token's `sub` as a `uuid`, or `NULL` when there is no user |
| `auth.role()` | `app_metadata.role`, falling back to the top-level `role` claim, then `anon` |
| `auth.claim(path)` | A nested claim by dotted path, used by `Claim<>` |
| `LoggedIn` | `(SELECT auth.uid()) IS NOT NULL` |
| `Owner<"owner_id">` | `(SELECT auth.uid()) = "owner_id"` |
| `Role<"admin">` | `(SELECT auth.role()) = 'admin'` |
