Because `auth.uid()` is `NULL` for a request with no user, an owner rule never matches an anonymous request, even on a row whose owner column is empty. The calls are wrapped in `SELECT` so Postgres evaluates them once per query rather than once per row.

To give a user an application role for `Role<>`, set `app_metadata.role` through the auth admin API with the service role key. Users cannot set it themselves.

### Pre-built UI

Two packages give you ready-made sign-in screens. Both use `useAuth()` from `@supatype/react`, so they must sit inside a `<SupatypeProvider>`.

| Package | Components |
| --- | --- |
| `@supatype/react-auth` | `LoginForm`, `SignUpForm`, `OAuthButton` |
| `@supatype/react-native-auth` | `LoginForm`, `SignUpForm`, `MagicLinkForm`, `OAuthButton`, `ResetPassword`, `AuthGate`, `AuthThemeProvider` |

#### Web

`src/SignIn.tsx`:

```tsx
import { SupatypeProvider } from "@supatype/react"
import { LoginForm, OAuthButton } from "@supatype/react-auth"
import { supatype } from "./supatype"

export function SignIn() {
  return (
    <SupatypeProvider client={supatype}>
      <LoginForm onSuccess={() => window.location.assign("/")} />
      <OAuthButton provider="github" redirectTo="http://localhost:5173/auth/callback" />
    </SupatypeProvider>
  )
}
```

The web forms are plain, unstyled markup: pass `className` and `labels` to fit your app. `OAuthButton` has a default style and an icon for GitHub, Google and Apple, which a `className` replaces. It sends the browser to the provider; the client finishes the sign-in on your callback page by itself, and `initialize()` tells you how it went.

#### React Native

`App.tsx`:

```tsx
import * as SecureStore from "expo-secure-store"
import * as WebBrowser from "expo-web-browser"
import * as Linking from "expo-linking"
import { SupatypeProvider } from "@supatype/react"
import { createNativeClient } from "@supatype/react-native"
import { AuthGate, LoginForm, OAuthButton } from "@supatype/react-native-auth"

const client = createNativeClient({
  url: process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_URL!,
  anonKey: process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY!,
  secureStore: SecureStore,
})
const redirectTo = Linking.createURL("auth/callback")

export default function App() {
  return (
    <SupatypeProvider client={client}>
      <AuthGate fallback={<><LoginForm /><OAuthButton provider="google" redirectTo={redirectTo} webBrowser={WebBrowser} /></>}>
        <>{/* your signed-in screens */}</>
      </AuthGate>
    </SupatypeProvider>
  )
}
```

`AuthGate` renders its children only when there is a session, and `fallback` otherwise. The native `OAuthButton` uses PKCE and opens the provider in `expo-web-browser`. Wrap the tree in `AuthThemeProvider` to change colours and spacing.

### Configuration

#### Email delivery

Confirmation, magic link and reset emails go through the `email` block in `supatype.config.ts`:

`supatype.config.ts`:

```ts
email: {
  provider: "smtp", // "console" | "smtp" | "resend" | "ses"
  smtp: { host: "smtp.example.com", port: 587, user: "apikey", pass: process.env.SMTP_PASS, admin_email: "no-reply@example.com" },
},
```

> **CONSOLE SENDS NOTHING:** `console`, the default, logs that a message would have been sent but leaves out the body, so the link is not in the log. To try magic links or password reset, configure a real provider.

For Resend, set `SUPATYPE_RESEND_API_KEY` and `SUPATYPE_RESEND_FROM` in `.env`. For SES, set `SUPATYPE_SES_FROM`; credentials come from the environment's AWS configuration.

#### Environment variables

The server reads the project's `.env` when it starts, so `SUPATYPE_*` auth variables placed there take effect after a restart. In the Docker stacks, a few values are set by the generated Compose file and are read from the plain names shown.

| Variable | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `JWT_SECRET` | Signs every token. Required for self-host. Change it and every issued token, including the anon and service role keys, stops working |
| `ANON_KEY`, `SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` | Keys signed with `JWT_SECRET`. `supatype keys --write` generates them |
| `SITE_URL` | Self-host: your app's URL, the default place users land after confirming or signing in |
| `SUPATYPE_URI_ALLOW_LIST` | Other URLs `redirectTo` may point at, comma-separated |
| `DISABLE_SIGNUP` (self-host), `SUPATYPE_DISABLE_SIGNUP` (native dev) | `true` stops new sign-ups |
| `SUPATYPE_MAILER_AUTOCONFIRM` | `true` skips email confirmation. On in dev, and on by default in self-host until you set it to `false` |
| `SUPATYPE_EXTERNAL_<PROVIDER>_*` | OAuth providers, see [above](https://www.supatype.com/docs/auth.html#oauth) |
| `SUPATYPE_EXTERNAL_ANONYMOUS_USERS_ENABLED` | Allow anonymous sign-in |
| `SUPATYPE_EXTERNAL_EMAIL_MAGIC_LINK_ENABLED` | `false` turns magic links off |
| `SUPATYPE_PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH` | Minimum password length, at least 6 |
| `SUPATYPE_EXTERNAL_PHONE_ENABLED`, `SUPATYPE_SMS_PROVIDER` | Phone sign-in. The provider is `twilio`, `twilio_verify`, `messagebird`, `textlocal` or `vonage` |

> **SELF-HOST:** Self-host turns auto-confirm on unless you set `SUPATYPE_MAILER_AUTOCONFIRM=false`. Set it, and configure email delivery, before you open sign-up to the public.

To create users from a seed file, see [Seeding users](https://www.supatype.com/docs/seeding.html#users).

## Storage

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/storage.html

Declare buckets in your schema, point file and image fields at them, and upload through the client. Who may read, upload, overwrite and delete is decided by Postgres from the bucket's rules.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### Declare a bucket

A bucket is a type alias for `Bucket<"id", { ... }>` in your schema. The [schema page](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#buckets) has the short version. Every key in the second argument is optional.

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
import type { Bucket, BucketLoggedIn, BucketOwner, BucketRole } from "@supatype/types"

export type Attachments = Bucket<"attachments", {
  accessMode: "private"
  accept: ["application/pdf", "image/*"]
  maxSize: "20MB"
  access: {
    read: BucketOwner
    create: BucketLoggedIn
    update: BucketOwner
    delete: BucketRole<"admin">
  }
}>
```

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `accessMode` | `"public"`, `"private"` or `"custom"`. Defaults to `"private"`. Only `"public"` serves files on a public URL. `"custom"` reads like `"private"` and is for buckets that set `s3BucketPolicy`. |
| `maxSize` | Largest file accepted, written as `"500KB"`, `"20MB"` or `"1GB"`. Units are B, KB, MB and GB, counted in 1024s. Anything else fails the push. |
| `accept` | Content types the bucket takes. Exact types such as `"image/png"`, or a wildcard such as `"image/*"`. Leave it out to accept any type. |
| `access` | The `read`, `create`, `update` and `delete` rules, covered [below](https://www.supatype.com/docs/storage.html#access). Any other key fails the push. |
| `s3BucketPolicy` | A raw S3 bucket policy as a JSON string, applied to the object store bucket in place of the default. |

`supatype push` and `supatype dev` register each bucket and write its settings. Changing `maxSize`, `accept` or `accessMode` and pushing again updates the bucket. Declaring the same bucket id twice with different settings fails the push.

### File and image fields

`ImageAsset<Bucket>` and `FileAsset<Bucket>` are fields that point at a file in a bucket. The column is JSONB holding the bucket and the path, and the generated type is `StorageReference`:

`supatype/generated`:

```ts
export type StorageReference = {
  bucket: string
  path: string
}
```

The field stores a reference, not the file. Upload the file first, then write its path to the row:

`typescript`:

```ts
const path = `${userId}/${file.name}`
const { error: uploadError } = await supatype.storage.from("attachments").upload(path, file)
if (uploadError) throw new Error(uploadError.message)

await supatype.from("post").update({ attachment: { bucket: "attachments", path } }).eq("id", postId)
```

- Always name the bucket. Without one, `ImageAsset` points at a bucket called `images` and `FileAsset` at one called `assets`, and neither exists unless you declare it.
- `ImageAsset<Covers, { localized: true }>` stores one reference per locale instead of one.
- Deleting a row does not delete its file, and deleting a file does not clear the field.

### Access rules

Each rule becomes a row level security policy on the table that records every stored file. The storage service runs each upload, overwrite, delete and list as the caller, so Postgres decides, the same way it does for your models.

| Rule | Who passes |
| --- | --- |
| `BucketPublic` | Everyone, including the anon key |
| `BucketLoggedIn` | Any signed-in user |
| `BucketOwner` | The user who uploaded the file. An overwrite keeps the original owner. |
| `BucketRole<"admin">` | Users whose `app_metadata.role` is `admin`, the same check as `Role` on a model |
| `BucketPrivate` | Nobody but the service role |

- A rule you leave out is refused, and the push prints a warning naming it.
- `update` and `delete` need a `read` rule beside them. Postgres only lets a caller change rows it can read, so without one they match nothing. The push warns about this too, even on a public bucket.
- `accessMode: "public"` serves files on the public URL without asking the `read` rule. Writes still go through `create`, `update` and `delete`.
- `list` returns only the files the caller may read. `remove` deletes only the files the caller may delete, leaves the rest in place and returns just the ones it removed.
- A refused write answers 401 to the anon key, because signing in might change the answer, and 403 to a signed-in user.

> **NOTE:** A bucket with no `access` of its own takes the access rules of each model that has a file or image field pointing at it. Owner rules then compare the caller with the file's uploader. Declare `access` on the bucket to keep its rules in one place.

### Upload

The [client page](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#storage) shows the basic calls. `upload` sends the file in one request with the caller's token.

`typescript`:

```ts
const { data, error } = await supatype.storage.from("attachments").upload(`${userId}/slides.pdf`, file, {
  contentType: "application/pdf",
  upsert: false,
})
if (error) console.error(error.status, error.message)
```

`file` may be a `File`, a `Blob` or an `ArrayBuffer`. On success `data` is `{ path }`.

Without `contentType` the client uses the `File`'s own type. If that is missing or generic, the service guesses from the extension (`.png`, `.pdf`, `.mp4` and other common types). The type is checked against `accept` before anything is stored.

With `upsert: true` an existing file at that path is replaced if the `update` rule allows it. The new bytes are stored alongside the old ones and swapped in when the row commits, so a reader never sees a half-written file.

| Status | Why |
| --- | --- |
| 401, 403 | The bucket's `create` rule (or `update`, for an overwrite) refused the caller |
| 404 | No bucket with that id |
| 409 | A file already exists at that path and `upsert` was not set |
| 413 | The file is larger than the bucket's `maxSize`, or the service limit when there is none |
| 415 | The content type is not in `accept`. The body lists the allowed types. |
| 507 | The upload would take the project past its total storage quota |

### Download and URLs

There are three ways to read a file. All three go through the storage service, which looks up the file's current version, so a URL keeps working after the file is overwritten.

| Method | Path | Who can use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `getPublicUrl(path)` | `/storage/v1/object/public/…` | Anyone, only on a bucket with `accessMode: "public"`. Builds the URL locally with no request. |
| `download(path)` | `/storage/v1/object/authenticated/…` | The caller, if the `read` rule allows. Returns a `Blob`. |
| `createSignedUrl(path, seconds)` | `/storage/v1/object/sign/…?token=` | Anyone holding the link until it expires |

A signed URL is only issued to a caller the `read` rule allows, and only for a file that exists. The expiry must be between 1 second and 7 days. The token is signed by the storage service and covers one bucket and one path. `createSignedUrls(paths, seconds)` signs several paths and reports an error per path.

`typescript`:

```ts
const bucket = supatype.storage.from("attachments")

const { data: blob } = await bucket.download(`${userId}/slides.pdf`)
const { data: link } = await bucket.createSignedUrl(`${userId}/slides.pdf`, 3600)
const { data: files } = await bucket.list(`${userId}/`, { limit: 50, offset: 0 })
```

`list` returns up to 100 entries unless you pass `limit`. Each entry has `name`, `size`, `mimetype`, the owner and timestamps.

The first argument to `list` is a folder. Folders inside it come first, then files, each in name order, and there is no sort option. Pass `search` to match names without regard to case. The result also carries `count`, the number of matching entries in all.

Every file the service serves carries `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600`. There is no setting per upload.

Public and private buckets differ in CORS too. A public bucket answers any origin. A private bucket sends no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so read its files from a browser with a signed URL or `download`.

`storage.listBuckets()` and `storage.createBucket(name, { public, fileSizeLimit, allowedMimeTypes })` need the service role key. Use them from a server or script, not a browser. In an app, declare buckets in the schema instead. The client has no call to change or delete a bucket. To change one, edit its declaration and push.

### Image transforms

`getPublicUrl` and `download` take a `transform` option. The service resizes and re-encodes the image on each request.

`typescript`:

```ts
const { data: { publicUrl } } = supatype.storage.from("covers").getPublicUrl(post.cover.path, {
  transform: { width: 800, height: 450, resize: "cover", format: "avif", quality: 70 },
})
```

| Option | Values | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `width`, `height` | 1 to 4096 pixels | the original size |
| `resize` | `cover`, `contain`, `fill`, `inside`, `outside` | `cover` |
| `format` | `webp`, `avif`, `png`, `jpeg` | `webp` |
| `quality` | 1 to 100 | 80 |

- A transform runs only when `width`, `height`, `format` or `quality` is set. `resize` on its own does nothing.
- Any transform re-encodes the image, as WebP unless you set `format`.
- Images are never enlarged past their original size.
- Files whose type is not `image/*` are served unchanged.
- The same query parameters (`width`, `height`, `resize`, `format`, `quality`) work when appended to a signed URL.
- Transformed responses carry `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` by default. Put a CDN in front if the same sizes are requested often.

### Limits and config

The storage service reads these environment variables. The self-host compose file sets the database, JWT and object store ones for you. The rest keep their defaults unless you set them on the `storage` service.

| Variable | Default | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TIER_MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE` | 52428800 (50 MB) | Largest file, in bytes, for a bucket with no `maxSize`. A bucket's `maxSize` always wins. |
| `STORAGE_QUOTA` | 1073741824 (1 GB) | Total bytes across every bucket. An upload past it gets 507. |
| `MAX_SIGNED_URL_EXPIRY` | 604800 (7 days) | Longest signed URL, in seconds |
| `DEFAULT_SIGNED_URL_EXPIRY` | 3600 | Expiry when a signing request names none |
| `SIGNED_URL_SECRET` | the JWT secret | Key that signs URL tokens. Changing it invalidates every signed URL. |
| `TRANSFORM_CACHE_TTL` | 3600 | `max-age`, in seconds, on transformed images |
| `S3_ENDPOINT`, `S3_REGION`, `S3_ACCESS_KEY`, `S3_SECRET_KEY`, `S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE` | the local SeaweedFS | Where the bytes are kept |

> **WARNING:** The 1 GB quota applies to self-hosted projects too, because the compose file does not set `STORAGE_QUOTA`. Raise it on the `storage` service if you expect to store more.

The service reads each upload fully into memory before storing it, so very large files cost memory on the storage container while they upload.

### Where files live

File metadata is a row in the `storage` schema of your project's Postgres. The bytes go to an S3-compatible object store, each upload under its own versioned key. Read files through the storage API, not the object store, because the key is not the path you uploaded to.

| Where you run | Where the bytes go |
| --- | --- |
| `supatype dev` (Docker, the default for new projects) | A SeaweedFS container, in the `storage-data` Docker volume. Its port is not published to your machine. `supatype dev --reset-db` keeps it. |
| `supatype dev` with `provider: "native"` | Plain files under `~/.supatype/projects/<name>/storage`, served by `supatype-server` |
| `supatype self-host compose up` | A SeaweedFS service in the stack, in the `storage-data` volume. Its S3 port, 8333, is published (`SUPATYPE_SEAWEEDFS_PORT` changes it) and needs the stack's credentials. There is no anonymous access. |

> **WARNING:** The native dev store is a stand-in. It checks that a bucket is public before serving a public URL, and that a request carries a token, but it does not apply bucket access rules, `maxSize` or `accept`, and it ignores transforms. Use the Docker provider to test storage rules before you deploy.

Back up the `storage-data` volume along with the database. A database dump holds the file records but not the bytes.

Removing a bucket from the schema drops its policies on the next push. The bucket and its files stay where they are.

## Realtime

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/realtime.html

Subscribe to inserts, updates and deletes on your tables over a WebSocket. Each change is checked against the subscriber's read access before it is sent.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### What is sent

The realtime service reads changes from Postgres logical replication, so every committed `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` is seen, whether it came from the API, Studio, a function or plain SQL. There is nothing to switch on per table. A change is only sent to clients subscribed to that table.

| Event | `new` | `old` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `INSERT` | the whole row | `null` |
| `UPDATE` | the whole row | the whole row as it was |
| `DELETE` | `null` | the whole row as it was |

Every table Supatype manages has `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`, so the write-ahead log carries the whole previous row. A table set up outside Supatype keeps Postgres's default identity, and its `old` can hold only the key.

Values arrive with the same types as a REST read. A `BigInt` column becomes a native `bigint`, and `Decimal` and `Money` stay exact strings.

### Read access

Realtime follows the same [access rules](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#access) as the REST API. For each change and each subscriber, the service checks with the subscriber's token, inside Postgres:

- Insert and update: the row is selected again, by its primary key, as the subscriber. If the `read` rule hides it, the change is not sent. The check sees the row as it is at that moment, so a row deleted straight after it was inserted is not sent either. With the Native provider or your own Postgres, the `read` rule is applied to the row in the change instead.
- Delete: the `read` rule is applied to the deleted row, as the subscriber, so a subscriber only hears of deletes of rows they could read. A delete on a table without `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`, or without a Supatype `read` rule, is not sent.
- Field rules: a column the subscriber may not read under a [field rule](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#field-rules) arrives as `null`, in both `new` and `old`. A filter on such a column is matched against the masked value, so it cannot be used to test a hidden value.
- Service role: sees every change unmasked.
- No token: receives no changes.

The row check uses the table's primary key. Inserts and updates on a table without one are not sent.

### Subscribe

`from(table).subscribe()` is the shortest path, shown on the [client page](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#realtime). The callback's rows are typed from your schema.

`typescript`:

```ts
const sub = supatype.from("comment").subscribe(
  (change) => {
    if (change.eventType === "INSERT") addComment(change.new)
    if (change.eventType === "UPDATE") replaceComment(change.new)
    if (change.eventType === "DELETE") removeComment(change.old?.id)
  },
  { event: "*", filter: `post_id=eq.${postId}` },
)

// later
sub.unsubscribe()
```

Each call opens its own channel, so two components watching the same table do not interfere. All channels share one WebSocket per client. The payload has `eventType`, `new`, `old`, `schema`, `table` and `commitTimestamp`.

#### Options

| Option | Values | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `event` | `"INSERT"`, `"UPDATE"`, `"DELETE"`, `"*"` | `"*"` |
| `filter` | `"column=op.value"`, several joined with commas | none |
| `schema` | the Postgres schema of the table | `"public"` |

#### Filters

A filter is checked on the server, so changes that do not match never reach the client. Several conditions joined with commas must all match. The operators are `eq`, `neq`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt` and `lte`.

- Values are compared by the column's type, as Postgres would compare them, so `salary=gt.100000` compares numbers. A column of a type the service does not recognise is compared as text.
- A null value, or one that cannot be read as the column's type, matches nothing.
- An operator not in that list is ignored, and the filter then matches every change.
- A delete is matched on `old`, the row as it was.

#### Channels

`supatype.realtime.channel(name)` is the lower-level form, for when you want the channel's status or want to mix changes with [broadcast and presence](https://www.supatype.com/docs/realtime.html#broadcast):

`typescript`:

```ts
const channel = supatype.realtime
  .channel(`post:${postId}`)
  .on("postgres_changes", { event: "INSERT", table: "comment", filter: `post_id=eq.${postId}` }, (change) => {
    showComment(change.new)
  })
  .subscribe((status) => console.log(status))
```

Status is `SUBSCRIBING`, `SUBSCRIBED`, `CHANNEL_ERROR`, `TIMED_OUT` or `CLOSED`. `CHANNEL_ERROR` means the server refused a request on the socket, such as a join. `TIMED_OUT` means the client gave up reconnecting. Render the status rather than assuming a channel is live: a subscription that stopped receiving looks the same as a quiet table. Pass `table` explicitly. Without it the channel name is read as `schema:table`.

A channel carries one table subscription. If you call `.on("postgres_changes", ...)` more than once on a channel, the first call's table, event and filter are what the server registers. Use one channel per table.

### Broadcast and presence

Broadcast sends a message to everyone else on a channel. Presence tells a channel who has joined and left. Neither touches the database.

`typescript`:

```ts
const room = supatype.realtime
  .channel(`cursor:${docId}`)
  .onBroadcast("move", (payload) => drawCursor(payload))
  .onPresence(({ joins, leaves }) => updateUsers(joins, leaves))
  .subscribe((status) => {
    if (status === "SUBSCRIBED") room.track({ name: displayName })
  })

room.broadcast("move", { x: 120, y: 48 })
```

- Only clients that have subscribed to the channel receive its messages. The sender does not get its own broadcast back.
- A presence entry is the payload you pass to `track`, plus `user_id` from the token. The server writes `user_id` last, so a payload cannot claim to be someone else. Every client without a signed-in user shares the `user_id` `anonymous`.
- Calling `track` again announces the new payload as a fresh join, so keep your own map of members keyed by `user_id`.
- A client that joins late hears about joins and leaves from then on. It is not sent the list of who is already there.
- A client leaves on `untrack()`, on unsubscribe and when its socket closes.
- Messages sent while the socket is not open are dropped, so send after `SUBSCRIBED`.

> **WARNING:** Broadcast and presence have no access rules. Anyone with your anon key who knows a channel's name can join it, read its messages and send to it. Do not put private data in a broadcast, and use a hard-to-guess channel name for anything you would not show the public.

### Framework hooks

`@supatype/react` exports `useSubscription`. It subscribes when the component mounts, unsubscribes when it unmounts, and re-subscribes when the channel name, event, table, schema or filter changes. The callback can change between renders without re-subscribing.

`tsx`:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react"
import { useSubscription } from "@supatype/react"
import type { TableRow } from "@supatype/client"

function Comments({ postId }: { postId: string }) {
  const [comments, setComments] = useState<TableRow<"comment">[]>([])
  const { status } = useSubscription<TableRow<"comment">>(`comments:${postId}`, {
    table: "comment",
    event: "INSERT",
    filter: `post_id=eq.${postId}`,
    callback: ({ new: row }) => { if (row) setComments((list) => [...list, row]) },
  })
  return <p>{status}: {comments.length} new</p>
}
```

It needs `SupatypeProvider` above it, which takes your client as `client`. Give each use its own channel name: two hooks with the same name share a channel.

`@supatype/vue` has `useSubscription(table, { event, filter })`, and `@supatype/svelte` and `@supatype/solid` have `createSubscription(table, { event, filter })`. These watch the `public` schema and return `data`, `error` and `status`, which is `"connecting"`, `"connected"`, `"disconnected"` or `"error"`. `data` starts empty and collects rows from the changes that arrive: inserts are added, updates replace the row with the same `id`, deletes remove it. They do not load the rows that already exist, so pair them with a query.

### Connection and auth

The client opens the socket at `/realtime/v1` on your project URL when the first channel subscribes, and closes it when the last one unsubscribes. It sends the current session's token, or the anon key when nobody is signed in.

`supatype.realtime.removeChannel(name)` leaves a channel by name. `supatype.realtime.disconnect()` closes the socket whatever is still subscribed, and reports `CLOSED` to every channel still registered.

When someone signs in, signs out or a different user signs in, the client reconnects with the new token and joins every channel again. Access is checked as the new identity from then on. A token refresh for the same user does not reconnect, so no changes are missed.

If the socket drops, the client retries after 1, 2, 4 seconds and so on, doubling each time, for up to 10 attempts. Channels report `SUBSCRIBING` while it retries and `TIMED_OUT` once it gives up. Changes made while the socket was down are not replayed, so refetch after a reconnect if you need the gaps filled.

### Config and requirements

Realtime needs Postgres with `wal_level = logical`, the `wal2json` plugin, and a database role allowed to create replication slots. The Postgres that `supatype dev` and the self-host stack run has all three. For a database you bring yourself, `supatype db check` tests for them.

If the database cannot do logical decoding, realtime does not stop the stack. The service stays up and serves broadcast and presence, change subscriptions deliver nothing, and `/health/ready` on the service answers 503 with the reason. When you run against your own database, set `database.external.realtime` to `false` in `supatype.config.ts` to leave the service out of the stack.

The service reads these environment variables. The self-host compose file sets the first three.

| Variable | Default | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DATABASE_URL` | required | The database to read changes from |
| `JWT_SECRET` | required | Verifies subscribers' tokens |
| `SLOT_NAME` | `supatype_realtime` | The replication slot the service creates and reads |
| `PORT` | 4000 | The port the service listens on |
| `REPLICATION_POLL_INTERVAL` | 100 | How often, in milliseconds, the slot is read |
| `SECURE_CHANNELS` | `true` | When `true`, a client must present a valid token before it can join a channel |

### Limits

- Changes are picked up by reading the replication slot every 100 ms, so expect that much delay on top of the network.
- While `supatype push` is changing the schema, the slot is not read. Changes made during the push are held in the slot and sent once it finishes.
- Each change costs one database query per subscriber, to check that subscriber's access. Many subscribers to a busy table means many queries.
- The replication slot keeps WAL until the service reads it. If the service is stopped for a long time while the database keeps writing, WAL builds up on disk.
- Subscriptions live in the service's memory. A restart drops every socket, and clients reconnect and join again.

## Functions

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/functions.html

A function is a TypeScript file in `functions/` that runs on Deno and answers HTTP at `/functions/v1/<name>`. It receives a standard `Request` and returns a standard `Response`.

### Where functions live

Functions sit in `functions/` at the project root. Each one is either a folder with an `index.ts` or a single `.ts` file. The name becomes the route.

| File | Route |
| --- | --- |
| `functions/send-invite/index.ts` | `/functions/v1/send-invite` |
| `functions/ping.ts` | `/functions/v1/ping` |
| `functions/_shared/email.ts` | none: shared code |

- Names starting with `_` or `.` are skipped, so `functions/_shared/` holds code every function can import with a relative path.
- `.d.ts` files are skipped.
- `_logs` is reserved by the worker, and the gateway refuses `/functions/v1/hooks` from outside, so do not use either name.

To use another directory, set `functions.path` in `supatype.config.ts`. It resolves against the project root.

`supatype.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "@supatype/cli"

export default defineConfig({
  project: { name: "my-app" },
  database: { provider: "docker" },
  server: { mode: "dev" },
  app: { mode: "none" },
  functions: {
    path: "functions",
  },
})
```

### Runtime

Functions run on Deno. Locally the CLI downloads Deno on first use. On a self-hosted stack they run in the `functions-worker` container, and `supatype-server` proxies `/functions/v1` to it.

The worker loads every function once at startup and serves them from one process. Invocations run concurrently: nothing per call is written to the process environment, so one slow function does not block another.

The CLI writes three files to help your editor: `functions/deno.d.ts`, `functions/tsconfig.json` and `functions/_shared/context.ts`. It also adds `functions` to the root `tsconfig.json` `exclude` list, so your app's type check skips Deno code. `context.ts` is rewritten by `init`, `functions new`, `push` and `dev`, so do not edit it.

### Write a function

Scaffold one with the CLI:

```sh
$ npx supatype functions new greet
```

A function default-exports a handler. It gets the request and a context object, and returns a `Response`. There is no Supatype package to import at runtime and no client injected for you.

`functions/greet/index.ts`:

```ts
import type { FunctionContext } from "../_shared/context.ts"

export default async function handler(req: Request, ctx: FunctionContext): Promise<Response> {
  if (req.method !== "POST") {
    return Response.json({ message: "Use POST" }, { status: 405 })
  }
  const { name } = (await req.json()) as { name?: string }
  return Response.json({ greeting: `Hello, ${name ?? "there"}`, region: ctx.region })
}
```

A thrown error becomes a `500` with `{ "error": "function_error", "message": "..." }`. An unknown name returns `404` with the list of available functions.

### The context object

The second argument carries what the function needs about its call and its project.

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `executionId` | A UUID unique to this call. Every log line the call writes carries it. |
| `functionName` | The route being served. |
| `url` | The project's API base URL, reachable from inside the function. |
| `anonKey` | The project's anon key. |
| `serviceRoleKey` | Only present when the project grants this function the service role. See [Service role](https://www.supatype.com/docs/functions.html#service-role). |
| `dbUrl` | A direct database URL, only when the deployment provides one. |
| `region` | `local` unless the deployment sets a region. |
| `env` | Your variables from the function env files. See [Environment and secrets](https://www.supatype.com/docs/functions.html#env). |

### Who is calling

The client sends the signed-in user's access token in the `Authorization` header. The function receives that header as it was sent. Nothing checks it for you, so a function that cares who is calling must ask auth.

`functions/whoami/index.ts`:

```ts
import type { FunctionContext } from "../_shared/context.ts"

export default async function handler(req: Request, ctx: FunctionContext): Promise<Response> {
  const authorization = req.headers.get("Authorization")
  if (!authorization) return Response.json({ message: "Sign in first" }, { status: 401 })

  const headers = { Authorization: authorization, apikey: ctx.anonKey }
  const res = await fetch(`${ctx.url}/auth/v1/user`, { headers })
  if (!res.ok) return Response.json({ message: "Not signed in" }, { status: 401 })

  const user = (await res.json()) as { id: string; email?: string }
  // Forward the same headers to REST and the user's access rules apply.
  const posts = await fetch(`${ctx.url}/rest/v1/post?select=title`, { headers })
  return Response.json({ id: user.id, posts: await posts.json() })
}
```

Forwarding the caller's token is the safe default: the database sees the user, not the function, and every [access rule](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html) still applies.

Do not decode the token yourself to read a role. Until its signature is checked, anyone can send a payload that says `"role": "admin"`. Ask `/auth/v1/user`, as above, which checks it. `supatype.auth.getUser()` on a client you create inside a function does not help here: it reads that client's own stored session, not the request's token, so it returns no user.

### Service role

A function is a public endpoint. By default it does not receive the service-role key, which reads and writes past every access rule. The worker removes the key from the environment before any function is imported, so `Deno.env` cannot reach it either.

To give a function the key, name it in `functions.serviceRole`. It then appears as `ctx.serviceRoleKey`.

`supatype.config.ts`:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  // ...
  functions: {
    serviceRole: ["send-invite"],
  },
})
```

`supatype push` refuses a name that matches no function, so a typo cannot silently grant nothing. `supatype doctor` lists the current grants.

> **LOCAL DEV:** The local router does not apply this list. Under `supatype dev` every function receives `ctx.serviceRoleKey`, and under `supatype functions serve` every function does when `SUPATYPE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` is set in your shell. Test that a function works without the key on a self-hosted stack.

### Environment and secrets

Variables for functions live in env files inside the functions directory:

- `functions/.env.local` is shared by every function.
- `functions/.env.<name>.local` applies to one function and overrides the shared file.

Read them from `ctx.env`. The files are read on each call, so a changed value takes effect without a restart. Keep them out of git.

```sh
$ npx supatype functions env set RESEND_API_KEY=re_123
$ npx supatype functions env list
$ npx supatype functions env unset RESEND_API_KEY
```

On a project that is not linked, these commands edit `functions/.env.local`. `list` masks the values.

`functions/send-invite/index.ts`:

```ts
const apiKey = ctx.env["RESEND_API_KEY"]
if (!apiKey) return Response.json({ message: "RESEND_API_KEY is not set" }, { status: 500 })
```

### Call a function

From your app, use `functions.invoke` on the client. It posts JSON to `/functions/v1/<name>` with the user's token and returns `{ data, error }`. A non-2xx response becomes `error`, using the `message` field from the body when there is one.

`typescript`:

```ts
const { data, error } = await supatype.functions.invoke("greet", { body: { name: "Alex" } })
```

`invoke` also takes `method` (default `POST`) and `headers`. A JSON response is parsed and anything else comes back as text. On a `401` the client refreshes the session once and retries. More in [Client: Functions](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#functions).

### Local development

`supatype dev` serves functions through the same gateway as the rest of the API when a functions directory exists. You do not run anything else.

To run functions on their own, with Deno watching for changes:

```sh
$ npx supatype functions serve
$ npx supatype functions invoke greet --local --data '{"name":"Alex"}'
```

`serve` listens on port `54321` by default; change it with `--port`. It loads `functions/.env.local` unless you pass `--env-file`. `invoke` sends a POST, prints the status and the response, and gives up after 30 seconds. `--auth` adds a test token to the request.

### Self-host

The self-host Compose file always includes a `functions-worker` service, built from the `supatype/functions-worker` image. It mounts the project read-only and serves `functions/` from it. There is no bundle or upload step: the files on disk are what runs.

The worker reads code once at startup, so restart it after changing a function:

```sh
$ docker compose -p supatype-<project> -f .supatype/self-host/docker-compose.yml restart functions-worker
```

`<project>` is your project name from `supatype.config.ts` in lower case, with spaces and other symbols replaced by `-`. `supatype self-host compose restart functions-worker` does the same and finds the project name for you. Env file changes do not need a restart.

On an unlinked project with a self-host Compose file, `supatype functions deploy` uploads nothing. It lists the functions it found on disk and prints that restart command.

The worker gets the anon and service-role keys from the stack. To give functions a database connection, set `SUPATYPE_FUNCTIONS_DB_URL`; it appears as `ctx.dbUrl`. It is off by default because a direct connection bypasses access rules, field masking and model hooks. Point it at a role you have restricted, or accept that.

Function logs are JSON lines on the container's output, each with the call's `request_id`, status and duration:

```sh
$ npx supatype self-host compose logs --service functions-worker
```

> **NOTE:** The Compose file mounts `functions/` at the project root. Keep the default path on a self-hosted stack.

### Model hooks

A model hook is a handler the API server calls around a write to one model: to check it, change it, refuse it, or react once it has happened. Hooks run on the same Deno worker as functions, but they are not public endpoints. They live in their own `hooks/` directory at the project root, the worker serves them under a `hooks/` route, and the gateway refuses that route from outside.

#### Triggers

| Key | Runs | Can |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `beforeChange` | Before an insert or update reaches Postgres | Let it through, replace the rows or the patch, or refuse it |
| `afterChange` | After an insert or update succeeded | React only. It cannot change or undo the write |
| `beforeDelete` | Before a delete reaches Postgres | Let it through or refuse it |
| `afterDelete` | After a delete succeeded | React only |

Hooks fire on writes to `/rest/v1/<table>`: `POST` and `PUT` are inserts, `PATCH` is an update, `DELETE` is a delete. That covers the client's `insert`, `upsert`, `update` and `delete`, including calls made with the service-role key. RPC calls, direct SQL, seeds and migrations do not fire them.

#### Declare a hook

Name the handler in the model's second argument. A string is the handler's directory name; an object adds options.

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
export type Post = Model<{
  id: UUID
  title: string
  // ...
}, {
  // access, versions, ...
  hooks: {
    beforeChange: "check-post"
    afterChange: { function: "notify-post"; timeout: 5000 }
  }
}>
```

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `function` | The directory under `hooks/`. |
| `timeout` | Milliseconds to wait for an answer. Default `2000`. |
| `onUnavailable` | What to do when the hook does not answer: a timeout, a connection failure, a `5xx`, a thrown error or an unreadable body. `"reject"` refuses the write, `"log"` lets it through and logs. Defaults to `"reject"` for `before*` hooks and `"log"` for `after*` hooks. |

`supatype push` refuses a schema whose hook names a directory with no `index.ts`, so a typo cannot leave a hook that never fires.

#### Write the handler

```sh
$ npx supatype hooks new check-post
$ npx supatype hooks list
```

`hooks new` creates `hooks/<name>/index.ts`. When a model already names it, the file is set up for that event; otherwise the command prints the line to add to the model. `hooks list` prints each `Model.event` with its handler and marks any whose handler is missing. `supatype doctor` reports the same.

Handlers import their types from `hooks/_supatype/hooks.ts`, which `push`, `dev` and `generate` write from your schema. Until the first push it does not exist, so a new handler will not compile yet. Do not edit it.

`hooks/check-post/index.ts`:

```ts
import { hook, type BeforeChange } from "../_supatype/hooks.ts"

const checkPost: BeforeChange<"post"> = async (ctx) => {
  if (ctx.operation === "insert") {
    if (ctx.rows.some((row) => row.title.trim() === "")) return { reject: "A post needs a title" }
    return { rows: ctx.rows.map((row) => ({ ...row, title: row.title.trim() })) }
  }
  if (ctx.patch.title !== undefined && ctx.patch.title.trim() === "") {
    return { reject: { message: "A post needs a title", status: 422, code: "empty_title" } }
  }
  return {}
}

export default hook(checkPost)
```

The type argument is the table name. `BeforeChange`, `AfterChange`, `BeforeDelete` and `AfterDelete` type the context from the model, and only tables that declare a hook are accepted.

| Context field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `table`, `operation` | The table and `insert`, `update` or `delete`. |
| `user` | `sub`, `role` and `email` from the caller's verified token, or `null` for an anonymous caller. |
| `requestId` | Matches the request in the server logs. |
| `rows` | An insert's rows, always an array. On `afterChange`, the written rows, only when the caller asked for them back with `.select()`. |
| `patch` | An update's changes. |
| `filter` | The request's filter on an update or delete, such as `id=eq.42`. A hook cannot change it. |
| `previous()` | Before an update or delete: fetches the rows about to change, up to 100, with `truncated: true` when there were more. They come back as stored, without field masking, so do not copy them into a refusal message. |

A `before*` handler returns `{}` to let the write through. `beforeChange` can return `{ rows }` for an insert or `{ patch }` for an update to replace what is written. `{ reject }` refuses the write: the caller gets your message with status `422`, or the `4xx` status you set. A thrown error is not a refusal: it counts as the hook not answering, and `onUnavailable` decides.

To keep a model's whole lifecycle in one directory, point several events at the same name and export `hooks({ beforeChange: checkPost, afterChange: notify })` instead of `hook(...)`. An event with no handler in that map lets the write through.

#### How hooks run

- The server reads the whole request body before any hook runs. A body over 1 MiB on a write to a hooked table is refused, rather than written without the hook.
- An `after*` hook runs once the caller already has its response. Its failures are logged and never reach the caller.
- A hook may write through the API, and those writes fire hooks too. A chain more than four hooks deep is refused with status `508`, so a hook that writes to its own table cannot loop forever.
- On a Docker stack the `functions-worker` container mounts `hooks/` next to `functions/`. When `supatype dev` runs on Docker, the worker restarts when a hook file changes. On a self-hosted stack, restart it after changing a hook, as for functions.

> **NOT A SECURITY BOUNDARY:** Direct SQL, seeds and migrations skip hooks. A rule every writer must follow belongs in the model's [access rules](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#access) or a constraint. Use hooks for application logic: enrichment, notifications, indexing, and checks the database cannot express.

### Limits

- The gateway waits up to two minutes for a function to start responding.
- The self-host worker sets no memory or CPU cap per function. Set container limits in Compose if you need them.
- Function names and bodies are not typed on the client.

## Seeding

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/seeding.html

A seed file describes the rows you want. Supatype checks it against your schema, orders the writes by foreign key and applies them in one transaction.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### Seed files

Put seed files in `seeds/`. They run in alphabetical order, so name them `01-authors.ts`, `02-posts.ts`. Without a `seeds/` folder, `seed.ts` at the project root runs instead.

Each file exports a default function. The function does not connect or await anything. It records the writes, and the engine applies them.

`seeds/01-blog.ts`:

```ts
import type { SeedContext } from "@supatype/cli/seed"

// Sign-in users are not seeded. Create them first, then use their ids:
//   supatype admin create-user --email alex@example.com --role editor
//   supatype admin list-users
const ALEX = "00000000-0000-4000-8000-0000000000a1"

export default async function seed({ db, expr, log }: SeedContext) {
  log("seeding authors, tags and posts")

  db.author.upsert({
    where: { id: ALEX },
    data: { id: ALEX, name: "Alex Rivera" },
  })

  db.tag.upsert({ where: { name: "news" }, data: { name: "news" } })

  db.post.upsert({
    where: { slug: "hello-world" },
    data: {
      title: "Hello world",
      slug: "hello-world",
      body: "Our first post.",
      kind: "news",
      views: expr.default(),
      published_at: expr.ago({ days: 1 }),
      author: { connect: { id: ALEX } },
      comments: { create: [{ user_id: ALEX, body: "First!" }] },
    },
  })
}
```

This uses the schema from the [Schema](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#relations) page.

### The builder

`db` has one property per table, typed from your schema. A wrong column or a missing required field fails to compile.

The types come from `supatype/generated/seed.ts`. `supatype generate`, `supatype dev` and `supatype push` write it. It needs no database, so it is gitignored and rebuilt on install.

The context also has `expr` (values the database computes), `log` (print a line) and `environment` (the `--environment` name, if given).

### Create and upsert

| Call | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `db.tag.create(data)` | Inserts one row. Running the seed again inserts it again |
| `db.tag.createMany(rows)` | Inserts many rows in one statement |
| `db.tag.upsert({ where, data })` | Inserts the row, or updates the row `where` names |

Use `upsert` for fixtures. Seeds get run again, and `upsert` makes that safe. `where` takes only columns that name one row: the primary key or a `Unique<>` column. A model with neither cannot be upserted, so give it a unique key.

Fields you leave out of `data` keep their current value when an upsert updates.

### Relations

Set a foreign key by naming the related row by any unique key:

`seeds/02-posts.ts`:

```ts
db.post.upsert({
  where: { slug: "second-post" },
  data: {
    title: "Second post",
    slug: "second-post",
    body: "More news.",
    kind: "news",
    author: { connect: { id: ALEX } },
  },
})
```

`create` and `upsert` return a reference you can use in later writes, such as `post.id`. It is not a value read from the database. The engine fills it in when it applies the seed.

`seeds/02-posts.ts`:

```ts
const tag = db.tag.create({ name: "release" })
log(`created a tag, referenced as ${String(tag.id)}`)
```

### Nested children

Write a row's children inside it with `create` or `createMany`. Their foreign keys are filled in for you.

Under an `upsert`, a child is written only if the parent has no child with the same values. So:

- Running the seed again adds nothing.
- A child whose values you changed is added beside the old one. The old one stays.
- A child that matches is not updated. To change one, upsert it on its own model by a unique key.
- Values the database computes, fields left out and `expr.default()` are not compared.

### Rich text and defaults

A `RichText` field takes a plain string. It becomes a one-paragraph document. Rich text inside a block is not converted, so write the full document there.

`expr` gives values the database works out when the seed runs:

`seeds/02-posts.ts`:

```ts
db.post.upsert({
  where: { slug: "launch-day" },
  data: {
    title: "Launch day",
    slug: "launch-day",
    body: "We are live.",
    kind: "news",
    views: expr.default(),
    published_at: expr.now({ days: 7 }),
    author: { connect: { id: ALEX } },
  },
})
```

`expr.now()`, `expr.ago({ days: 1 })` and `expr.startOf("day", { days: 30, hours: 9 })` are times. They only fit date fields.

`expr.default()` sets the column's own default. It is sent as `{ "$default": true }`. Leaving a field out of an upsert keeps the old value. `expr.default()` resets it. It only fits columns that have a default.

Leave `id` out and the database makes one.

### Sign-in users

A seed cannot create sign-in users. Users live in the auth schema, which the seed builder does not reach. Create them first, then put their ids in the seed:

```sh
$ supatype admin create-user --email alex@example.com --role editor
$ supatype admin list-users
```

`create-user` also gives the user a Studio role (`admin` if you do not pass `--role`). `list-users` prints each id.

For app users with no Studio access, sign them up through the client's `auth.signUp`, or create them in Studio under Authentication > Users with Studio access set to "No access".

A `SupatypeAuthUserId` field with `onDelete` has a foreign key to the user, so the user must exist before the seed runs.

### Many-to-many rows

Many-to-many relations have no nested write. The rows live in the junction table, which the builder does not list. Write them with `db.$sql`, which runs in the same transaction:

`seeds/03-tags.ts`:

```ts
db.$sql(
  `insert into post_tag (post_id, tag_id)
   select p.id, t.id from post p, tag t
   where p.slug = $1 and t.name = $2
   on conflict do nothing`,
  ["hello-world", "news"],
)
```

The statement runs at its position in the file, after every write above it, so it can read the rows those writes made.

Each param binds by its JSON type: a string as `text`, a whole number as `bigint`, any other number as `double precision`, a boolean as `boolean`, and an object or array as `jsonb`. A column of another type needs a cast on its placeholder, such as `$1::uuid`. That includes an id taken from an earlier write, such as `post.id`, which binds as text:

`seeds/03-tags.ts`:

```ts
const post = db.post.create({ slug: "hello-world", title: "Hello" })
db.$sql(
  `insert into post_tag (post_id, tag_id)
   select $1::uuid, t.id from tag t where t.name = $2
   on conflict do nothing`,
  [post.id, "news"],
)
```

> **ONE PARAM PER PLACEHOLDER:** Pass exactly one param for each of `$1` to `$n` in the statement. A count that does not match is refused before anything runs. A param is a value, so write expressions such as `now()` in the statement itself.

### Running seeds

```sh
$ supatype seed                    # every file in seeds/
$ supatype seed seeds/02-posts.ts  # one file
$ supatype seed --atomic           # all files in one transaction
$ supatype seed --status           # what ran, when, and what it wrote
```

Each file is one transaction. Without `--atomic`, a failure in the third file leaves the first two applied, and the report says so.

Errors name your schema, such as `Tag.name is already taken`, with the file and position. Exit code `1` means a seed failed. Exit code `2` means the run could not start.

A seed writes the model's own table, so rows on a drafts model are seeded as published.

## Studio

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio.html

Studio is the admin app that ships with every Supatype stack. It builds content editors from your models and gives developers the API docs, a SQL runner and the database history in one place.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### Open Studio

Studio is served at `/studio/` on the project's gateway.

- **Local, Docker (the default):** `supatype dev` prints it in the **Services running** panel as `http://localhost:<gateway-port>/studio/`. The port is `SUPATYPE_KONG_PORT` in `.env`.
- **Self-hosted:** `http://<your-host>:<gateway-port>/studio/`, or `/studio/` on your domain once HTTPS is on. See [Self-host](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#self-host).
- **Local, Native:** `supatype dev` does not start Studio with the Native provider.

Sign in with an email and password. The first admin comes from `SUPATYPE_ADMIN_EMAIL` and `SUPATYPE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` in `.env`, as described in [Local development](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#local-dev). Add more people with `supatype admin create-user`.

Studio also offers every OAuth provider the project has enabled. To offer only some, name them in `supatype.config.ts`:

`supatype.config.ts`:

```ts
studio: { auth: { providers: ["github"] } }
```

Signing in is not enough on its own. Every person also needs a [Studio role](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html).

### Finding your way

The sidebar holds the dashboard, Models, Database, Media & Storage, Authentication, Edge Functions, Realtime and Observability, plus Settings. Entries marked as coming soon open a placeholder page and do nothing yet.

**Jump to** in the top bar searches pages, users and records.

If the newest schema push was refused or failed, a notice shows above every screen. It says that nothing was applied and links to that push in the migration history. It goes away once a push applies.

### Editing content

Studio reads your schema after each push and builds an editor for every model. There is nothing to configure: add a model, save, and it appears under **Models**.

#### The list

Each model opens on a list of its records. Columns you can sort have sortable headers. Fields wrapped in `Searchable<T>`, or named in the model's `searchable: [...]` option, get a search box. Tick rows to delete several at once, after a confirmation. **Create Post** (named after the model) opens an empty form.

#### The record editor

Each field gets an input that matches its type: text, numbers, dates, slugs, selects, relations, JSON, code, images, files, rich text and blocks among them. The model's name in Studio comes from `label` and `labelPlural` in its options. A form also has **Duplicate** and **Delete**, and Delete asks first.

A `Slug<"title">` field follows the title on a new record. A model with hooks shows "This post has custom logic that runs on save."

A singleton model (`singleton: true`) is listed under **Globals** and opens straight into its one record.

If the project has more than one locale, a language switcher appears in the top bar on content screens.

#### Model tabs

Each model has tabs beside the editor:

| Tab | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| Schema | The model's fields as the database has them |
| Rules | Field bounds, constraints and indexes, as the database enforces them |
| Data | A table browser for the model's table, with filters, inline edits and a record inspector |
| API | REST examples for this model |
| GraphQL | GraphQL examples for this model |
| Cache | The model's cached REST responses |

Editors do not see Schema or Rules. Cache is for admins and developers.

### Rich text and blocks

A `RichText` field opens a rich text editor with a toolbar for bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, headings 1 to 3, paragraphs, bullet lists and numbered lists. The field stores a Lexical document.

A `Blocks<T>` field is a list of sections. An editor adds a block by type, fills in its fields, and can move or duplicate it. See [Slugs, rich text and blocks](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#content) for how they are declared and stored.

To render a rich text field in React, pass the stored value to `RichText` from `@supatype/react`:

`src/PostBody.tsx`:

```tsx
import { RichText } from "@supatype/react"
import type { TableRow } from "@supatype/client"

export function PostBody({ post }: { post: TableRow<"post"> }) {
  return <RichText content={post.body} as="article" />
}
```

### Media and files

**Media & Storage** lists your buckets. Each bucket has two tabs:

- **Files:** browse folders, upload files (or drop them on the page), create folders, and download or delete files. **Details** shows a file's size, type, owner, dates and its public URL.
- **Policies:** the bucket's access rules. Who can read or change them is on [Studio roles](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html#matrix).

Declare buckets in your schema with `Bucket<>` so they are versioned with everything else. Studio can create one by hand, but warns first and recommends the schema instead. See [Storage](https://www.supatype.com/docs/storage.html).

An image field in the record editor takes a dropped file, an **Upload**, or **Select from bucket**, which browses the bucket the field names. A localized image field uploads one image per locale.

### Drafts and publishing

On a model with `versions: { drafts: true }` (see [Drafts and versions](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#drafts)), the editor's side panel holds the publishing controls:

- **Save draft** saves without changing what readers see. On a new record the first save creates it.
- **Publish** makes the saved draft live, saving any unsaved edits first.
- The menu beside Publish has **Schedule publish...** (and **Change schedule...** or **Cancel schedule** once one is set), **Discard changes**, which returns the draft to the published version, and **Unpublish**, which keeps the content as a draft.

A status badge shows Draft, Published, Scheduled or Partly published, and "Changed" when there are edits since publishing. With several locales a record can be published, and unpublished, per language.

A draft may leave a required field empty. Studio asks before saving it, and it cannot be published until the field is filled.

Who sees drafts and the publish controls is set by `publishing.draft_visibility`. See [Drafts and publishing](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html#drafts) in Studio roles, which also covers saving drafts from the Data tab.

### Version history

A model with `versions` keeps a history of each record. On a model with drafts, open it with **History** in the publishing panel. Each version shows when it was saved, by whom, and its state: Live, Scheduled, Pending draft or Superseded. Select a version to compare its fields with the newest one.

- **Restore as draft** brings the version back as the current draft. Nothing goes live until it is published.
- **Publish this version** restores it and publishes it in one step.

A model without `versions` says so, and keeps no history.

### Live preview and preview links

Tell Studio where each model renders in your app with `admin.livePreview`, keyed by model name. Field names in braces are filled from the record:

`supatype.config.ts`:

```ts
admin: {
  livePreview: {
    Post: { urlPattern: "/preview/{slug}" },
  },
},
```

A path is enough when the same stack serves your app (`app.mode` is `static` or `proxy`). With `app.mode: "none"` give a full URL. `supatype push` refuses a path in that mode.

#### Live preview

With this set, the editor gets a **Live preview** button. It opens your page in a side panel and sends the unsaved form values to it on every change. Read them with `useLivePreview`:

`src/PostPreview.tsx`:

```tsx
import { useLivePreview } from "@supatype/react"

export function PostPreview({ post }: { post: { title: string } }) {
  const { data, isPreview } = useLivePreview({ initialData: post, model: "Post" })
  return <h1>{data.title}{isPreview && " (preview)"}</h1>
}
```

`model` is the schema's model name, as in `admin.livePreview`. The hook only accepts messages from the window that frames the page, at Studio's origin. By default that is the origin of the client in `SupatypeProvider`. If Studio is served somewhere else, pass `studioOrigin`.

#### Share a preview

On a saved record, **Share a preview** makes a link for someone without an account. Choose how long it lives: 15 minutes, 1 hour, 1 day or 7 days. The link is your preview URL with a `preview` query parameter. Studio lists the links it has made, and each can be revoked.

On the preview page, create a client with that code as `previewCode` and read the draft with `.draft()`. The code is the client's whole credential: it cannot be combined with `serviceRoleKey`. See [Drafts and publishing](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#drafts) in Client.

### API docs

**Settings > API > REST** opens the REST docs. They are built from your models plus the auth and storage endpoints. Each endpoint lists its parameters, an example body and response, and a curl example. Filter by category or table, or search.

**Try it** sends a real request and shows the response headers and body. It asks who to send as: yourself, anonymous, the service role or a pasted token. See [Send as](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html#send-as).

The REST section also has Settings and Cache tabs for admins and developers.

### GraphQL explorer

The GraphQL page sends queries to `POST /graphql/v1`. Pick a model to start from a list query, edit it, and press **Run**. It uses the same Send as choice as Try it. Each model's GraphQL tab has examples for that model.

### SQL runner

**Database > SQL Runner** runs SQL against the project. Press **Run Query**, or Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac).

- Each run opens a result tab with its time. Export a result as CSV or JSON.
- Statements that drop, empty or overwrite data (`DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `DELETE`, `UPDATE`, and an `ALTER` that drops something or turns off row level security) ask first and name what they change.
- `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)` draws the plan as a tree.
- Query History lists earlier runs in this session.

> **FULL ACCESS:** Queries run as `supatype_sql_editor`, which has the rights of the role that owns your tables. Row level security does not apply and masked columns show in full. It is not a superuser. Every query is recorded. Only admins and developers can open it.

### Database, migrations and schema objects

Editors do not see the Database pages. The SQL runner is for admins and developers only.

| Page | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| Overview | A diagram of your tables and their relations |
| Tables, Views, Triggers, Indexes, Constraints, Types, Roles, Extensions | The database's objects of that kind |
| Migrations | Every push: its status, number of changes, when it was applied, who pushed it and the engine version. Open one to see its schema changes and its SQL. Filter by status and date, or search by name or id |
| Schema objects | Every object Supatype manages, from the managed-object ledger, with its status (managed, adopted or released) and a link to the migration that last changed it |
| Seeds | Each recorded `supatype seed` run: file, status, rows written, time and duration |

Adopted and released objects come from [supatype adopt](https://www.supatype.com/docs/cli.html#schema). Seed runs are covered in [Seeding](https://www.supatype.com/docs/seeding.html#run).

### Logs

Function logs are on the **Edge Functions** page. Pick a function and open its **Logs** tab. Live tail is on by default. Turn it off to read recent logs by time range, with optional auto-refresh. A deployment that runs functions inside the server process has no worker to tail, so Studio shows recent logs instead.

The same page has an **Invoke** tab to call a function, and **Environment Variables**. See [Functions](https://www.supatype.com/docs/functions.html).

> **NOTE:** Under Observability, API request logs are not recorded yet. Auth, storage, realtime and Postgres logs are coming soon.

### Other screens

| Screen | For |
| --- | --- |
| Dashboard | Totals and recent activity for users, records, storage and the database |
| Authentication | Users (including their Studio access), access policies, providers, configuration and email templates. Configuration is read-only: change those settings in `.env` and restart the stack. A template saved under Email Templates is kept in the database until **Reset to default** removes it. See [Auth](https://www.supatype.com/docs/auth.html) |
| Settings | API keys, CORS origins and database settings |
| Realtime | Channels, clients, a live stream and a broadcast tester, where the deployment's control plane supports the inspector |

### Roles

What each person can see and change in Studio depends on their Studio role: admin, developer, editor or viewer. Admins and developers work with full access. Editors and viewers work within the role's limits, and field masks still apply to them.

The full table, field masking, Send as and how to give someone a role are on [Studio roles](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html).

## Studio roles

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html

Everyone who signs in to Studio has a Studio role. The role decides which screens they see and what they may change.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### The four roles

A self-hosted project has four Studio roles:

**Admin**: Everything, including giving and removing Studio roles.

**Developer**: Everything an admin can do, except Studio roles.

**Editor**: Content and files. No schema, SQL or settings.

**Viewer**: Reads content, files, schema and logs. Changes nothing.

Supatype Cloud adds owner and billing roles for the organisation. On a self-hosted project those two grant nothing, and the CLI refuses any role but the four above.

> **NOTE:** A Studio role is separate from your app. It grants nothing in your own application, and `Role<>` rules in the schema do not read it.

### What each role can do

The server checks every Studio request against this table.

| Can | Admin | Developer | Editor | Viewer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Browse content and download files | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Edit content, upload and delete files | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| See the schema, migrations and access rules | Yes | Yes | No | Yes |
| See logs | Yes | Yes | No | Yes |
| Push the schema | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Deploy functions, hooks and secrets | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Use the SQL editor | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Work with full access | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Use the realtime inspector | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Manage API keys, CORS and domains | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Manage the app's users | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Create, change and delete buckets | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Give and remove Studio roles | Yes | No | No | No |

> **SQL EDITOR:** The SQL editor runs as the database owner. Row level security does not apply there, and masked columns show in full. Every query is recorded.

> **BUCKET RULES:** A bucket's access rules page is part of "see the access rules". Viewers see it read-only. Editors cannot open it today. A change in progress shows it to editors read-only too. Only admins and developers can change the rules.

### Full access and Studio mode

Admins and developers work with full access. Studio acts for them as the service role, so your app's access rules and field masks do not apply. An amber "Full access" banner shows while project rows are on screen. Every change is recorded.

Editors and viewers work in Studio mode. Your app's row rules are skipped, so the Studio role decides which rows they reach. Field rules still apply, so masked columns stay masked. Every change is recorded.

There is no switch for this on content screens. To see data as an app user would, use [Send as](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html#send-as).

### Field masking

A column with a [field rule](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#field-rules) shows a padlock in Studio:

- A padlock alone: the value is hidden from you.
- A padlock with a question mark: the column is restricted per record, and this value is hidden or empty.
- A value with a small padlock: you can see it, but other callers may not.

In forms, a column you cannot read shows the padlock. A column you can read but not write is disabled. Admins and developers see every value with the small padlock, because masks do not apply to full access.

### Send as

The API page's Try it, the GraphQL explorer and a function's Invoke tab ask who to send the request as:

| Choice | Sends | Offered to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Me (default) | Your own token. Your app's access rules apply to you | Every role |
| Anonymous | The anon key, as a visitor who is not signed in | Every role |
| Service role | The service role. No rules apply. The key never reaches the browser | Admins and developers |
| A token I paste | A token you paste, such as a test user's | Every role |

The choice applies to one request and is not remembered. The Invoke tab is on the Edge Functions page, which only admins and developers can open.

### Drafts and publishing

On a model with drafts, the record editor shows Save draft and Publish. Its menu also schedules, discards and unpublishes.

Admins, developers and editors see drafts by default. Change this with `publishing.draft_visibility` in `supatype.config.ts`. A role that cannot see drafts does not get the publish controls.

In the Data browser, saving a cell or adding a row on a drafts model asks first:

- Save as draft: the change is stored as a draft, and a new row is created unpublished. The cell keeps the live value with a Draft badge until the record is published.
- Save and publish: the change goes live now, with any earlier draft changes to that record. A new row is created and published.

> **DELETES ARE PERMANENT:** Deleting a row in the Data browser deletes it for good. It does not make a draft.

### Giving someone a role

In Studio, open Authentication > Users. The Studio access column shows each user's role. An admin can change it there, or choose No access. Other roles see it read-only. Your own row cannot be changed.

Create User has a Studio access choice too. Only admins see it.

From the command line:

```sh
$ supatype admin create-user --email sam@example.com --role editor
$ supatype admin set-role --email sam@example.com --role viewer
$ supatype admin list-users
```

`create-user` makes a new sign-in user with a Studio role. `--role` is `admin`, `developer`, `editor` or `viewer`, and defaults to `admin`. It asks for the password if you leave out `--password`. `supatype dev` and `supatype push` make sure a first admin exists.

> **CLI:** The CLI writes the database directly. It does not run the checks Studio runs, such as keeping the last admin.

### Only admins change admins

- Only admins give, change or remove Studio roles.
- A developer cannot change an admin's account: no disabling, deleting, password or email changes, MFA changes, signing out or sending links. The server refuses with "Only a Studio admin can change another admin's account."
- Nobody can change their own Studio role or remove their own access.
- The last admin cannot be removed. Make someone else an admin first.

## Deploy to a VM with GitHub Actions

Source: https://www.supatype.com/deploy-vm-github-actions.html

Create a project on your laptop, push it to GitHub, run the stack on a VM with Docker Compose, and ship schema and frontend changes on every push to `main`.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### What you will have

- One repository with `supatype.config.ts`, shared by local development and the VM.
- A VM running `supatype self-host compose`, with the gateway serving HTTPS for your domain on ports 80 and 443.
- A GitHub Action that connects over SSH, pulls, migrates, rebuilds static files and restarts Compose.

> **SCOPE:** This guide covers self-hosting only. Supatype Cloud is a separate product.

### Create the project locally

On your machine, with Node.js 22 or later.

#### 1. Scaffold

```sh
$ npm install -g @supatype/cli
$ mkdir my-blog && cd my-blog
$ supatype init
```

`init` installs dependencies and writes generated secrets and API keys to `.env` for local development.

#### 2. Add a static frontend

```sh
$ supatype app add --static ./public
$ npm install -D vite
# in package.json: "build": "vite build", with output in public/
```

Commit `supatype.config.ts`. You do not run `app add` again on the server.

Give the deployment its domain while you are here. The gateway gets a Let's Encrypt certificate for it itself, so there is no reverse proxy to set up:

```sh
$ supatype add domain example.com --email you@example.com
```

This writes `server.mode`, `server.domain` and `server.tls` to `supatype.config.ts`. `supatype dev` ignores them, so local development stays on `http://localhost`. See [Self-hosting](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#self-host) for the details.

#### 3. Develop, then push to GitHub

```sh
$ supatype dev
$ supatype push
```

Optionally proxy to Vite from a gitignored `supatype.local.config.ts` while production stays `static`. See [Deploy changes](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#deploy-changes).

```sh
$ git init
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Initial Supatype project"
$ git branch -M main
$ git remote add origin git@github.com:YOUR_USER/my-blog.git
$ git push -u origin main
```

### Prepare the VM

A one-time setup on Ubuntu 22.04 or similar, with SSH access.

#### 4. Install the tools and clone

`vm`:

```sh
# Docker: https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/
# Node.js 22 or later (Ubuntu's own nodejs package is older): https://nodejs.org/en/download
$ sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git
$ sudo npm install -g @supatype/cli

$ sudo mkdir -p /opt/my-blog
$ sudo chown "$USER":"$USER" /opt/my-blog
$ cd /opt/my-blog
$ git clone git@github.com:YOUR_USER/my-blog.git .
```

#### 5. Write the production secrets

Create `/opt/my-blog/.env` on the server and never commit it. Generate each `CHANGE_ME` with `openssl rand -base64 48 | tr -d '/+='`, use a different value for each, and set your public URL. Compose refuses to start while any of the passwords or secrets is missing.

`/opt/my-blog/.env`:

```ini
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://supatype_admin:CHANGE_ME@localhost:5432/my-blog
POSTGRES_USER=supatype_admin
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=CHANGE_ME     # the same value as in DATABASE_URL
POSTGRES_DB=my-blog
AUTHENTICATOR_PASSWORD=CHANGE_ME
SUPATYPE_SQL_EDITOR_PASSWORD=CHANGE_ME
SUPATYPE_CONTROL_PLANE_SECRET=CHANGE_ME
JWT_SECRET=CHANGE_ME            # at least 32 characters
ANON_KEY=
SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=
API_EXTERNAL_URL=https://example.com
SITE_URL=https://example.com
```

Then run `supatype keys --write` in `/opt/my-blog`. It signs `ANON_KEY` and `SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` from this `JWT_SECRET` and adds the `VITE_SUPATYPE_URL` and `VITE_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY` copies your frontend build reads. Keys from your laptop will not work here, because they were signed with a different secret.

#### 6. First boot

`vm`:

```sh
$ cd /opt/my-blog
$ npm install
$ supatype self-host compose render
$ supatype self-host compose up -d
$ supatype push
$ npm run build
$ supatype self-host compose render
$ supatype self-host compose up -d
```

Before this, point an A record for `example.com` at the VM and open ports 80 and 443 in its firewall. Then open `https://example.com`, with Studio at `/studio/`. Without a domain in `supatype.config.ts`, the gateway is on `http://YOUR_VM_IP:18473` instead. Backups, logs and rollbacks are covered in [Running in production](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#production).

### Repository secrets

In your repository, open **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions** and add:

| Secret | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `VM_HOST` | Public IP or hostname of the VM |
| `VM_USER` | SSH user, for example `ubuntu` |
| `VM_SSH_KEY` | Private key (PEM) that can log in as `VM_USER` |
| `DEPLOY_PATH` | Project directory on the VM, for example `/opt/my-blog` |

> **NOTE:** The workflow never uploads `.env`. Production secrets stay on the VM.

### The workflow

Add `.github/workflows/deploy-self-host.yml` to your repository:

`.github/workflows/deploy-self-host.yml`:

```yml
name: Deploy self-host

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy over SSH
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1.2.0
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.VM_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.VM_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.VM_SSH_KEY }}
          script_stop: true
          script: |
            set -euo pipefail
            cd "${{ secrets.DEPLOY_PATH }}"
            git fetch origin main
            git reset --hard origin/main
            npm ci
            supatype push
            npm run build
            supatype self-host compose render
            supatype self-host compose up -d
```

On every push to `main` the VM pulls the latest code, applies schema migrations, rebuilds `public/` and refreshes Compose.

> **NOTE:** `supatype push` reads `DATABASE_URL` from the VM's `.env`, which points at the Compose Postgres on `localhost:5432`. If you would rather not install the CLI globally on the VM, use `npx @supatype/cli` in the script.

### Verify the pipeline

#### 7. Push a change

```sh
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Add posts and update the landing page"
$ git push origin main
```

Watch the run under **Actions** on GitHub. When it succeeds, load your gateway URL and check that the schema and static files changed.

#### If something fails

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| SSH fails | The firewall allows port 22, and `VM_SSH_KEY` matches the VM's `authorized_keys`. |
| `supatype push` fails | Compose is up, and `DATABASE_URL` points at `localhost:5432`. |
| Site unchanged | `npm run build` writes to the directory in `app.static_dir`, then re-run `compose render` and `up -d`. |

> **RATHER NOT RUN IT YOURSELF?:** Supatype Cloud runs the same stack for you, and it is coming soon. [Join the waiting list](https://www.supatype.com/#cloud), or [book a call](https://www.supatype.com/#contact) about self-hosting with support.

## Coming from Supabase

Source: https://www.supatype.com/from-supabase.html

Supatype runs on Postgres with row level security, a REST and GraphQL API, auth, storage, realtime and functions, so most of what you know carries over. The difference is where it starts: you write TypeScript types and access rules, and Supatype writes the SQL, the policies and the client types from them.

### What maps to what

| In Supabase | In Supatype |
| --- | --- |
| `create table` in SQL migration files | A `Model<>` type in `schema/index.ts`. See [Models](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#models) |
