| RLS policies written with `create policy` | An `access` rule for `read`, `create`, `update` and `delete` on the model. Supatype turns it into row level security. See [Access rules](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#access) |
| Column privileges and views to hide a column | A field rule under `access.fields`. A caller who may not read the column gets `null`. See [Field rules](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#field-rules) |
| Applying migrations, then running `supabase gen types` | `supatype dev` locally, `supatype push` elsewhere. Both apply the schema and write the client types |
| `supabase-js` | `@supatype/client`, imported from the generated `supatype/generated/client`. See [Create the client](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#setup) |
| Studio table editor | Supatype Studio: a form for each model built from its fields, version history and drafts, a media library, plus database views and a SQL runner. See [Studio roles](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html) |
| Storage buckets and policies on `storage.objects` | A `Bucket<>` type with the same four rules as a model. See [Storage buckets](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#buckets) |
| Supabase Auth | Supatype's auth service, reached through `supatype.auth`: sign up, password, magic links, OAuth, one-time codes and MFA. See [Auth](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#auth) |
| Realtime `postgres_changes` on a channel | `supatype.from("table").subscribe()`. Broadcast and presence use `supatype.realtime.channel(name)`. See [Realtime](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#realtime) |
| Edge Functions on Deno | Functions on Deno, called at `/functions/v1/<name>` and from `supatype.functions.invoke`. See [Functions](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#functions) |

### What you stop writing

- SQL for tables, columns, indexes, foreign keys and enums. The model type declares them.
- One RLS policy per operation, with `using` and `with check` kept in step by hand. One rule per operation does both.
- Migration files. A push compares your schema with the database, shows the plan and asks before anything that can lose data. `supatype diff` shows the plan without applying it.
- A separate type generation step after each migration. Types are written on every `supatype dev` save and every `supatype push`.
- Bucket policies in SQL. A bucket's rules sit next to the models in the schema.

### Before and after

A posts table where anyone reads published posts, and authors read and change their own.

#### Supabase

`supabase/migrations/20260101000000_posts.sql`:

```sql
create table public.posts (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  author_id uuid not null references auth.users (id) on delete cascade,
  title text not null,
  status text not null default 'draft' check (status in ('draft', 'published'))
);

alter table public.posts enable row level security;

create policy "Read published or own" on public.posts for select
  using (status = 'published' or (select auth.uid()) = author_id);
create policy "Insert own" on public.posts for insert to authenticated
  with check ((select auth.uid()) = author_id);
create policy "Update own" on public.posts for update to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = author_id) with check ((select auth.uid()) = author_id);
create policy "Delete own" on public.posts for delete to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = author_id);
```

```sh
$ supabase migration up
$ supabase gen types typescript --local > database.types.ts
```

#### Supatype

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
import type { Model, UUID, SupatypeAuthUserId, Default, Owner, Any, Eq, Literal } from "@supatype/types"

export type Post = Model<{
  id: UUID
  author_id: SupatypeAuthUserId<{ onDelete: "cascade" }>
  title: string
  status: Default<"draft" | "published", "draft">
}, {
  access: {
    read: Any<[Eq<"status", Literal<"published">>, Owner<"author_id">]>
    create: Owner<"author_id">
    update: Owner<"author_id">
    delete: Owner<"author_id">
  }
}>
```

```sh
$ supatype dev
```

The table is named `post`, from the type name. Set `tableName: "posts"` in the second argument to keep the old name. Because the `create` rule is `Owner<"author_id">`, the column defaults to the caller's id, so an insert can leave it out.

#### The query

`before: supabase-js`:

```ts
import { createClient } from "@supabase/supabase-js"
import type { Database } from "./database.types"

const supabase = createClient<Database>(url, key)
const { data, error } = await supabase.from("posts").select("id, title").eq("status", "published")
```

`after: @supatype/client`:

```ts
import { createClient } from "../supatype/generated/client"

const supatype = createClient({ url, anonKey })
const { data, error } = await supatype.from("post").select("id, title").eq("status", "published")
```

The query builder reads the same way. The differences are in the setup: `createClient` takes one object with `url` and `anonKey`, and it comes from the generated file, so there is no type argument to pass.

### Small differences in the client

- Session fields are camel case: `session.accessToken`, `session.refreshToken`, `session.expiresAt`.
- Row changes are subscribed from the table: `supatype.from("comment").subscribe(cb, { event: "INSERT" })`. Each change reaches only subscribers allowed to read that row.
- `error` is a plain object with `message` and, when known, `code`. An insert an access rule refuses returns `42501`. See [Errors](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#errors).
- A function is a Deno module with a default export, `handler(req, ctx)`. The project URL and keys come from `ctx`, not the environment. `supatype functions new hello` writes one to start from.

### Bringing an existing database

To bring the data too, dump only your own schema, usually `public`. Supabase's own schemas, such as `auth` and `storage`, are not yours to restore over Supatype's. The CLI has no restore command, so load the dump with `psql`. `supatype dev` points `DATABASE_URL` in `.env` at the local database. Rows with a foreign key to `auth.users` need their users to exist first, so move users before those rows.

```sh
$ pg_dump -h db.yourproject.supabase.co -U postgres -d postgres --schema=public --no-owner --no-privileges -f supabase-dump.sql
$ psql "$(grep '^DATABASE_URL=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)" -f supabase-dump.sql
```

`supatype pull` reads a live database and drafts `schema/index.ts` from it. It prints the draft unless you pass `--out`.

```sh
$ supatype pull --connection "postgres://..." --out schema/index.ts
$ supatype diff
```

Read the draft before you push it. It is a starting point, not a translation:

- Every model is drafted with `Public` for all four rules. Your RLS policies are not read. Replace each rule with the one you mean.
- An `id` column of type uuid is drafted as `SupatypeAuthUserId`. Change it to `UUID` on every table whose id is not a user's id.
- A uuid column ending in `_id` is drafted as a plain `UUID` with a comment suggesting a relation. Make it a `RelatedTo<>`, or a `SupatypeAuthUserId` when it points at a user.
- Model names come from table names, and the table name is derived back from the model name. Add `tableName` wherever the two differ, such as a plural table name.
- Tables whose names start with `_` are skipped.

#### Adopting tables Supatype did not create

A table that already exists was not created by Supatype, so a push refuses it: the access rules your schema declares for it would not be in force. In a terminal, `supatype push` says which tables, then asks `Adopt them now?`. Answer yes and it shows what adoption will take and asks `Adopt these?` before it changes anything. After adopting, it pushes again.

`--yes` does not answer the adoption questions. Agreeing to a push is not agreeing to take over tables, so with `--yes` or without a terminal the push stops and prints the command to run instead:

```sh
$ supatype adopt                      # shows what it would take, then asks
$ supatype adopt --key table:post     # adopt only the objects you name
$ supatype push
```

`supatype adopt --release <object>` tells every push to leave an object alone. `--reclaim <object>` hands it back. Objects are named the way `supatype doctor` names them: `kind:table.name`, or `kind:name` for a table.

### What does not carry over

- **Your SQL migrations.** Supatype does not replay `supabase/migrations`. It plans changes from the schema and records the migrations it applies.
- **Your RLS policies.** They are rewritten as access rules. Rules are types, and there is no raw SQL escape hatch, so a policy the rule types cannot express needs another approach, such as a hook or a function.
- **Generated types.** Delete `database.types.ts`. The client types come from the generated `supatype/generated` files.
- **Function entry points.** The handler shape differs, so each function's entry needs a small rewrite. The code inside, being Deno, mostly stays.
- **Function names and bodies in the client are not typed**, unlike tables.

### Users and files

There is no command to import auth users or stored files. Plan each as its own step.

For users, either ask them to sign up again, or copy their rows. Supatype's auth server descends from the same code as Supabase Auth and keeps the same bcrypt hashes in `auth.users.encrypted_password`, so copied rows keep their passwords. The two `auth` schemas are not guaranteed to match column for column. Copy the columns you need, at least `id`, `email`, `encrypted_password`, `email_confirmed_at` and `raw_user_meta_data`, and try it on a copy first. This path is not a supported tool.

For files, declare each bucket in your schema and push. Then download each file from Supabase and upload it with a client that holds the service role key, from a one-off script on a server:

`scripts/copy-files.ts`:

```ts
import { createClient } from "../supatype/generated/client"

const supatype = createClient({
  url: process.env.PUBLIC_SUPATYPE_URL!,
  anonKey: process.env.ANON_KEY!,
  serviceRoleKey: process.env.SERVICE_ROLE_KEY!,
})

export async function copyFile(sourceUrl: string, path: string): Promise<void> {
  const res = await fetch(sourceUrl)
  // An expired link or a private bucket answers with an error page, which must not become the file.
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${path}: the source answered ${res.status}`)
  const { error } = await supatype.storage.from("avatars").upload(path, await res.blob(), { upsert: true })
  if (error) throw new Error(`${path}: ${error.message}`)
}
```

## Coming from Prisma

Source: https://www.supatype.com/from-prisma.html

Prisma gives you tables, migrations and a typed client from one schema file. Supatype does the same from TypeScript types, then goes on to access rules, an API, an admin UI, auth and storage, which with Prisma you write yourself.

### What maps to what

| In Prisma | In Supatype |
| --- | --- |
| `model` in `schema.prisma` | A `Model<>` type in `schema/index.ts`. See [Models](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#models) |
| `prisma migrate dev` | `supatype dev`: each save is applied to the local database |
| `prisma migrate deploy` | `supatype push`, which shows the plan and asks before anything that can lose data |
| `prisma migrate diff` | `supatype diff`: the plan, without applying it |
| `prisma db pull` | `supatype pull`: a draft schema from a live database |
| `prisma generate` | Types are written by `supatype dev` and `supatype push`. `supatype generate` writes them on their own |
| Prisma Client | `@supatype/client`. See [Client](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html) |
| Prisma Studio | Supatype Studio, a CMS built from the schema. See [Studio roles](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html) |
| `prisma db seed` | `supatype seed`. See [Seeding](https://www.supatype.com/docs/seeding.html) |

#### Field by field

| Prisma | Supatype |
| --- | --- |
| `String @id @default(uuid())` | `id: UUID`. The database fills it in |
| `String?` | `Optional<string>`. Every other field is `NOT NULL` |
| `@unique` | `Unique<T>` |
| `@default(value)` | `Default<T, value>` |
| `enum Status { draft published }` | `"draft" \| "published"` |
| `Json` | `JSON<T>`, typed as `T` in the client |
| `@relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id])` | `RelatedTo<Author>`, which adds the column `author_id` |
| The list side, `posts Post[]` | `HasMany<Post>`. It adds no column |
| An implicit many-to-many | `ManyToMany<Tag>`, one junction table for the pair |
| `@@index`, `@@map` | `indexes` and `tableName` in the model's second argument |

The full list is in [Field types](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#fields) and [Relations](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#relations).

### Before and after

#### Prisma

`prisma/schema.prisma`:

```prisma
enum Status {
  draft
  published
}

model Author {
  id    String @id @default(uuid())
  email String @unique
  name  String
  posts Post[]
}

model Post {
  id       String @id @default(uuid())
  title    String
  status   Status @default(draft)
  author   Author @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  authorId String
}
```

`before: Prisma Client`:

```ts
const posts = await prisma.post.findMany({
  where: { status: "published" },
  select: { id: true, title: true, author: { select: { name: true } } },
})
```

#### Supatype

`schema/index.ts`:

```ts
import type {
  Model, UUID, Email, Unique, Default, SupatypeAuthUserId,
  RelatedTo, HasMany, Public, Owner, Any, Eq, Literal,
} from "@supatype/types"

export type Author = Model<{
  id: SupatypeAuthUserId
  email: Unique<Email>
  name: string
  posts: HasMany<Post>
}, {
  access: { read: Public; create: Owner<"id">; update: Owner<"id">; delete: Owner<"id"> }
}>

export type Post = Model<{
  id: UUID
  title: string
  status: Default<"draft" | "published", "draft">
  author: RelatedTo<Author, { required: true; onDelete: "cascade" }>
}, {
  access: {
    read: Any<[Eq<"status", Literal<"published">>, Owner<"author_id">]>
    create: Owner<"author_id">
    update: Owner<"author_id">
    delete: Owner<"author_id">
  }
}>
```

`after: @supatype/client`:

```ts
const { data: posts, error } = await supatype
  .from("post")
  .select("id, title, author(name)")
  .eq("status", "published")
```

The author's id is a sign-in user's id, so each author row belongs to a user. The `access` blocks are the part Prisma has no place for: they become Postgres row level security, so the same query returns only what the caller may see, whether it runs on your server or in the browser.

### What Supatype adds

- **Access rules in the database.** Each model's rules become row level security, and field rules mask single columns. They hold for REST, GraphQL, realtime and the client alike. See [Access rules](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#access).
- **An API you do not write.** Every model with access rules is reachable over REST and GraphQL. A model with no `access` at all is not.
- **A client that runs in the browser.** It holds the anon key and the user's session, not a database connection.
- **Studio.** A form for each model built from its fields, drafts and version history, a media library, and roles for the people who edit content. See [Studio roles](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html).
- **Auth, storage, realtime and functions** in the same project. Buckets are declared in the schema next to the models. See [Auth](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#auth), [Storage](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#storage), [Realtime](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#realtime) and [Functions](https://www.supatype.com/docs/client.html#functions).

### Bringing an existing database

`supatype pull` drafts a schema from a live database. Prisma's `_prisma_migrations` table is skipped, along with any table whose name starts with `_`.

```sh
$ supatype pull --connection "postgres://..." --out schema/index.ts
$ supatype diff
```

Prisma's defaults and Supatype's differ, so expect to edit the draft:

- Prisma names a table after the model, such as `"Post"`. Supatype derives the table name from the model name in snake case, so `Post` means `post`. Add `tableName: "Post"` to keep the existing table.
- A field's name is its column's name. A relation's column is the field name plus `_id`, and there is no option to name it otherwise, so a Prisma `authorId` column does not line up with an `author` relation. Keep it as a plain field, or rename the column.
- Every drafted model has `Public` for all four rules. Replace them with the rules you mean before you push.
- An `id` column of type uuid is drafted as `SupatypeAuthUserId`. Change it to `UUID` on every table whose id is not a user's id.
- Prisma fills `@default(uuid())` in the client, and stores a `String` id as text unless you used `@db.Uuid`. Such an id is drafted as a string, not a `UUID`.

The first push refuses tables that exist and that Supatype did not create. In a terminal it offers to adopt them: it asks `Adopt them now?`, shows what adoption will take, and asks again before changing anything. `--yes` does not answer those questions. Without a terminal, run `supatype adopt` and then push again. See [What a push refuses](https://www.supatype.com/docs/schema.html#push).

### What does not carry over

- **Other databases.** Supatype runs on Postgres 17 only. MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server and MongoDB projects need moving to Postgres first.
- **Your migrations folder.** Supatype does not read `prisma/migrations`. It compares the schema with the database and plans the change itself.
- **Nested writes and transactions.** The client writes one table per call and has no transaction API. Put a write that must touch several tables at once in a function.
- **Raw queries.** There is no `$queryRaw`. Studio has a SQL runner for one-off queries.
- **Client extensions and middleware.** Logic that ran around every query belongs in access rules, model hooks or functions.

> **PRISMA 8:** Prisma 8, in release candidates at the time of writing, replaces `schema.prisma` with `contract.prisma` and renames the migrate commands. The mapping above is to Prisma 7.

## Postgres

Source: https://www.supatype.com/postgres.html

PostgreSQL 17 with the extensions an app needs, our own extensions, and safe defaults. It is the database under every Supatype project. Use it on its own too. Open source under the PostgreSQL License, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.

### Run it

```sh
docker run -d \
  --name supatype-postgres \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your-password \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  supatype/postgres:17-latest
```

The default superuser is `supatype_admin`, set with `POSTGRES_USER`.

### Our extensions

- [`pg_keyspace`](https://www.supatype.com/postgres/pg-keyspace.html): Redis, inside your Postgres.
- [`pg_topics`](https://www.supatype.com/postgres/pg-topics.html): Kafka topics, with no broker to run. Not in the image yet.
- [`pg_guard`](https://www.supatype.com/postgres/pg-guard.html): Superuser features, without the superuser.
- [`supatype_mask`](https://www.supatype.com/postgres/supatype-mask.html): Hide a column per row, not per table.

### Also included

| Extension | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `PostGIS` | Geography and geometry types, and spatial queries. |
| `pgvector` | Vector embeddings and similarity search. |
| `pg_graphql` | A GraphQL API over your schema. |
| `pg_net` | Async HTTP requests from triggers and functions. |
| `pgjwt` | JWT signing and checking in SQL. |
| `pg_cron` | Scheduled jobs inside Postgres. |
| `pg_safeupdate` | Stops UPDATE and DELETE with no WHERE clause. |
| `pg_plan_filter` | Rejects queries over a cost limit. |
| `wal2json` | Logical decoding as JSON, for realtime. |

### Safe defaults

- Row level security is on by default.
- Passwords are stored as scram-sha-256.
- The ordinary postgres role is not a superuser.
- A table you make by hand in public is not granted to anon or authenticated until you grant it.
- pg_guard loads on every connection, so roles can manage extensions without SUPERUSER.
- A failed migration stops the container, so no client reaches a half-migrated database.

Migrations run on first boot and on every start after, so pulling a newer tag over an existing volume applies what is new. `supatype migrate doctor` checks that the important ones took effect.

### Tags

| Tag | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `supatype/postgres:17-latest` | The newest PG17 release. Moves only when a release is tagged. |
| `supatype/postgres:x.y.z` | One release, pinned and never changed. |
| `supatype/postgres:latest` | The same image as 17-latest. |
| `supatype/postgres:develop` | The newest build of the develop branch. |

Not using Docker? Each release also ships native archives for Linux, macOS and Windows, and the image runs under CloudNativePG. The [supatype/postgres repository](https://github.com/supatype/postgres) covers both.

## pg_keyspace

Source: https://www.supatype.com/postgres/pg-keyspace.html

Redis, inside your Postgres. pg_keyspace runs a Redis and Valkey compatible server inside Postgres. Your Redis client connects unchanged, and SQL reads the same keys.

### Why pg_keyspace

Most teams that need a cache run Redis or Valkey beside Postgres. That is a second stateful service to deploy, secure, monitor and back up. It has its own users, its own backups and its own idea of what is current.

pg_keyspace moves the cache into Postgres. A background worker speaks the Redis protocol (RESP2 and RESP3) over a shared-memory keyspace. redis-cli, ioredis, redis-py and valkey-go connect without changes. The same bytes are readable from SQL, and a read inside a backend takes about 9 ns.

It keeps what you already trust. Redis AUTH maps to a Postgres role, keys can be scoped per tenant, and the wire can use TLS. Durability is a setting per key prefix, from memory only to fsync before the reply. Persisted keys live in ordinary tables, so your Postgres backups and point-in-time recovery cover the cache too.

### An example

```sh
# Any Redis client works. Here, redis-cli on the RESP port.
redis-cli -p 6379 SET session:42 '{"user":"ada"}' EX 3600
redis-cli -p 6379 HSET user:42 name Ada plan pro
redis-cli -p 6379 ZADD leaderboard 120 ada 95 grace
redis-cli -p 6379 ZRANGE leaderboard 0 -1 WITHSCORES

# The same keyspace, read from SQL in the same database.
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "
  SELECT convert_from(supacache.get('session:42'), 'UTF8');"

# Write from SQL with a 60 second TTL, read it back over RESP.
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "SELECT supacache.set('flag:beta', 'on', 60);"
redis-cli -p 6379 GET flag:beta            # "on"

# Tell RESP subscribers something from SQL, say from a trigger.
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "
  SELECT supacache.publish('orders', 'shipped:42');"

# Hit rate, entries and memory, as a normal Postgres view.
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "SELECT * FROM supacache.pg_stat_keyspace;"
```

### pg_keyspace or a separate Redis or Valkey cluster

|  | a separate Redis or Valkey cluster | pg_keyspace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you run | A separate service or cluster to deploy, patch, secure and monitor. | A background worker inside the Postgres you already run. |
| Clients | Any Redis client. | Stock Redis clients, unmodified, over RESP2 or RESP3, including client-side caching. |
| Cache hit (GET, closed loop) | About 35 to 39 µs. | About 34 to 39 µs. |
| Pipelined throughput, one worker | About 537k to 628k ops/s. Higher on GET. | About 500k to 556k ops/s. More workers scale it out. |
| SQL access to the same data | None. It is a separate datastore. | Yes. supacache.get reads the same shared memory, about 9 ns in a backend. |
| Auth and tenancy | Redis ACLs, in a separate user store. | AUTH maps to a Postgres role. Keys and channels are scoped per tenant. TLS can reuse the Postgres certificate. |
| Durability | RDB snapshots and AOF, set for the whole instance. | Four tiers, from memory only to a synchronous standby, chosen per key prefix. |
| Backups | A separate artefact on a separate schedule with a separate restore. | Persisted keys are Postgres tables, so base backups and point-in-time recovery include them. |
| Monitoring | A Redis exporter to deploy and wire up. | pg_stat_keyspace views, granted to pg_monitor. Existing Postgres collectors read them. |
| Command and type surface | Wider. Adds streams, scripting, HyperLogLog and geo. | Strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, Bloom and Cuckoo filters, pub/sub and transactions. |
| Maturity | Mature and battle-tested, with a large ecosystem. | New, with a focused feature set. |

### What it does not do

- No streams, Lua scripting (EVAL) or blocking commands such as BLPOP yet. They are planned with no date, and a client that sends them gets ERR unknown command. Check for both before treating it as a drop-in.
- FUNCTION and FCALL are declined. HyperLogLog is not planned, and geo is declined in favour of PostGIS.
- Valkey has a higher raw write ceiling with persistence off. If you need maximum single-node write throughput or mature cluster tooling today, stay on Valkey.
- It is opt-in. The library has to be preloaded, so turning it on is a restart. Its shared memory is reserved at startup whether or not the cache is full.
- The default tier is ephemeral, so keys live in memory and are lost on restart. The durable tiers wait for a Postgres commit: a median of 1.04 ms per write against 39 µs for ephemeral in the published benchmark.
- The replicated tier cannot be mixed with other tiers on one instance. It applies to the whole keyspace or not at all.
- A streaming standby serves no RESP until it is promoted. On a replica the keyspace is reachable only through SQL.
- With more than one worker and a persisted tier, clients need their cluster constructor, unless owner recovery addressing is on. Changing the worker count is a restart, and there is no online resharding.
- The PostgREST row cache is off by default and eventually coherent. After an UPDATE, another session can read the previous row for 200 ms plus decode time by default, and for longer when many databases share the invalidation pool.
- Pub/sub crosses instances only for channels you opt in, and delivery is at most once. Bloom and Cuckoo filters are reachable over RESP only, with no SQL functions yet.

### Use it on its own

pg_keyspace ships in the [supatype/postgres](https://www.supatype.com/postgres.html) image. Use the image as your Postgres, with or without the rest of Supatype.

```sh
# pg_keyspace ships in the image but is not loaded by default.
# SUPATYPE_KEYSPACE_ENABLED=1 adds it to shared_preload_libraries
# and creates the extension in POSTGRES_DB on first start.
docker run -d \
  --name supatype-postgres \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your-password \
  -e SUPATYPE_KEYSPACE_ENABLED=1 \
  -e SUPATYPE_KEYSPACE_DURABILITY=ephemeral \
  -e SUPATYPE_KEYSPACE_DURABILITY_OVERRIDES='acme:=durable' \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:6379:6379 \
  supatype/postgres:17-latest

redis-cli -p 6379 PING                     # PONG

# RESP asks for no password until you set one, so the port above
# listens on this machine only. Before you open it up:
#   SELECT supacache.set_credential('app', 'secret', 'app_role', 'app');
```

### With Supatype

Every Supatype project runs on this image, with migrations, access rules, an API, a typed client and Studio generated from your TypeScript types. [Run it locally](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#local-dev) in a few commands. The full reference is the extension's [README](https://github.com/supatype/postgres/blob/develop/extensions/pg_keyspace/README.md).

## pg_topics

Source: https://www.supatype.com/postgres/pg-topics.html

Kafka topics, with no broker to run. pg_topics turns a Postgres table into a Kafka topic. Stock Kafka clients produce and consume on a port the extension opens, and SQL can do the same work inside your own transaction.

> **SOURCE ONLY:** Not in the supatype/postgres image yet. Build it from source in the supatype/postgres repository.

### Why pg_topics

Most teams that want an event log already run Postgres. The usual answer is a second system: a Kafka cluster with its own backups, patching, users and monitoring. Then every write that must also publish an event needs an outbox table to keep the two in step.

pg_topics puts the topic in the database. Each topic is a table. A Kafka client logs in with a Postgres role and its password, over TLS, and produces and consumes as it would against a broker. A SQL user calls topic.publish inside the same transaction as the rest of their writes, so the event commits with the data or not at all.

History stays queryable with SQL, Postgres grants are the only permission system, and an optional worker keeps a normal table current from a topic so you can read the latest state with SELECT. It suits a team that needs up to tens of thousands of events a second, not hundreds of thousands.

### An example

`orders.sql`:

```sql
-- A topic is a table whose name ends in _q. A band is a Kafka partition.
SELECT topic.create_topic('shop.orders_q', band_count => 4);
SELECT topic.grant_consume('shop.orders_q', 'billing_service');

-- Publish in the same transaction as your own writes. No outbox table.
BEGIN;
UPDATE shop.stock SET count = count - 1 WHERE sku = 'A-100';
SELECT topic.publish('shop.orders_q', '{"order_id": 2, "sku": "A-100"}', key => 'customer-42');
COMMIT;

-- Read it back in SQL.
SELECT * FROM topic.fetch('shop.orders_q',
  band => topic.band_for('customer-42', 4), from_offset => 0);

-- Or with a stock Kafka client: SASL_SSL, PLAIN, a Postgres role and its password.
--   kafka-console-consumer --bootstrap-server kafka.example.internal:9092 \
--     --consumer.config client.properties --topic shop.orders_q --from-beginning

-- Alert when ok = false.
SELECT * FROM topic.health();
```

### pg_topics or a Kafka cluster

|  | a Kafka cluster | pg_topics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you run | A broker cluster beside your database, with its own backups, patching and monitoring. | Your PostgreSQL 17 server. There is no broker to run, back up or patch. |
| Publish with a database write | Needs an outbox table, or a second write that can fail on its own. | topic.publish joins your transaction. A ROLLBACK removes the record. |
| Access control | Its own users and ACLs, kept apart from the database's. | Postgres roles and grants. A Kafka client logs in as a role. |
| Reading history | Consume the log, or copy it into a database first. | Every topic is a table that SQL can query, on the primary or a standby. |
| Current state per key | Log compaction. | No compaction. A sync worker keeps a normal table current instead. |
| Throughput | Scales out across brokers. | One primary does all the writes. About 10,000 records a second with low latency, and up to about 44,000 at top speed, on the test machine. |
| Transactions and exactly once | Supported. | Not supported. Idempotent producers are supported. |
| Monitoring | JMX metrics. | SQL views and topic.health(). There are no JMX metrics. |

### What it does not do

- PostgreSQL 17 only. Other versions are not built or tested.
- A record value must be valid JSON, and a key must be UTF-8 text of 40 characters or fewer.
- A topic name is schema.table_q, and clients must use the full name. A producer aimed at orders gets TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED.
- No Kafka transactions or exactly once. A transactional.id gets TRANSACTIONAL_ID_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED.
- No log compaction, and no size based retention. Retention is by time only and drops whole partitions.
- The band count is fixed when you make the topic. There is no CreatePartitions.
- Only SASL PLAIN over TLS. No SCRAM, OAUTHBEARER, GSSAPI, mutual TLS or plain text.
- Classic consumer groups only. The KIP-848 protocol, static membership and share groups are not offered.
- Kafka Connect in distributed mode, Kafka Streams and Schema Registry make compacted topics, so they are expected to fail. They are not tested.
- One broker and one primary. Publish throughput does not grow with more machines. Standbys give failover and SQL history reads.
- Fetch returns the value as jsonb prints it, so a signature over the raw bytes does not match.
- librdkafka clients must set partitioner=murmur2_random, or keyed records land on different bands from a SQL publish.
- A restart of PostgreSQL makes every consumer group rebalance once.

### Use it on its own

Not in the supatype/postgres image yet. Build it from source in the supatype/postgres repository. Its README covers the install.

`postgresql.conf`:

```ini
# Add pg_topics to your existing shared_preload_libraries list.
shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_topics'
pg_topics.databases = 'app'
pg_topics.failover_is_fenced = on

# The Kafka port speaks TLS only.
pg_topics.tls_cert_file = '/etc/pg_topics/server.crt'
pg_topics.tls_key_file  = '/etc/pg_topics/server.key'
pg_topics.advertised_host = 'kafka.example.internal'

# Restart PostgreSQL, then in the app database run:
#   CREATE EXTENSION pg_topics;
```

### With Supatype

Every Supatype project runs on this image, with migrations, access rules, an API, a typed client and Studio generated from your TypeScript types. [Run it locally](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#local-dev) in a few commands. The full reference is the extension's [README](https://github.com/supatype/postgres/blob/develop/extensions/pg_topics/README.md).

## pg_guard

Source: https://www.supatype.com/postgres/pg-guard.html

Superuser features, without the superuser. pg_guard lets a non-superuser role create extensions, event triggers and publications. It still cannot make itself a superuser.

### Why pg_guard

Postgres keeps a lot behind SUPERUSER. Event triggers, publications, foreign data wrappers and extensions such as hstore all need it. So teams hand out SUPERUSER, and with it the power to read server files, run programs and change any role.

pg_guard adds one privileged role. When that role creates a superuser-only object, pg_guard switches to a configured superuser, creates it, hands ownership back and switches back. Event triggers it creates skip superusers and reserved roles, so they cannot be used to escalate. It cannot create a SUPERUSER role or grant the attribute.

Everything lives in postgresql.conf. There are no tables, functions or security labels in your database, so upgrades are simple and a reload applies a change. It is derived from supautils and runs in every supatype/postgres container.

### An example

`pg_guard.sql`:

```sql
-- postgres is not a superuser here. It is a member of
-- supatype_privileged_role, the image's pg_guard.privileged_role.
set role postgres;
select current_setting('is_superuser');  -- off

create extension hstore;                 -- in pg_guard.privileged_extensions
create publication app_changes for all tables;
set session_replication_role = replica;  -- in privileged_role_allowed_configs

-- An event trigger. The function must not be superuser-owned.
create function log_ddl() returns event_trigger
language plpgsql as $$
begin
  raise notice 'ddl by %', current_user;
end;
$$;
create event trigger log_ddl on ddl_command_end
  execute procedure log_ddl();

create role escalate superuser;
-- ERROR:  permission denied to create role
```

### pg_guard or handing out SUPERUSER

|  | handing out SUPERUSER | pg_guard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Extensions that need a superuser | Only a superuser can create hstore, postgres_fdw and the like. | Non-superusers can create, update and drop any extension listed in pg_guard.privileged_extensions. Others behave as normal. |
| Event triggers | Superuser only. A trigger fires for every role, superusers included. | The privileged role can create them. They are skipped for superusers and reserved roles. |
| Publications and FDWs | Superuser only. | The privileged role creates them and owns them. |
| Becoming a superuser | The role already is one. | The privileged role cannot create a SUPERUSER role or add the attribute to one. |
| Roles your services log in as | Any superuser can alter or drop them, or grant pg_read_server_files. | Reserved roles cannot be altered or dropped by non-superusers. Reserved memberships cannot be granted. |
| Where the rules live | Role attributes and grants, set role by role. | postgresql.conf only. Settings take effect on a reload, with no objects added to the database. |

### What it does not do

- Event triggers made by the privileged role do not fire when it creates publications, foreign data wrappers or extensions.
- Those event triggers are skipped for superusers and reserved roles, so they do not see DDL from those roles.
- It does not restrict superusers. Keep the real superuser for the platform, not for people.
- It loads per session through session_preload_libraries. A role given its own list without pg_guard runs without it. supatype migrate doctor checks this for authenticator.
- Extension parameter overrides support the schema parameter only. Custom scripts run before-create and after-create only.
- Settings are cluster-wide. You cannot give one database a different list.
- It is not in the cross-compiled linux-arm64 native archive. The Docker image is not affected.

### Use it on its own

pg_guard ships in the [supatype/postgres](https://www.supatype.com/postgres.html) image. Use the image as your Postgres, with or without the rest of Supatype.

```sh
# pg_guard is on by default in the image
docker run -d --name supatype-postgres \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your-password -p 5432:5432 \
  supatype/postgres:17-latest

# Preloaded for every session, with its settings in their own file:
#   session_preload_libraries = 'pg_guard'
#   include = '/etc/postgresql-custom/pg_guard.conf'
docker exec supatype-postgres \
  cat /etc/postgresql-custom/pg_guard.conf

# Make one of your roles privileged (as supatype_admin)
psql -h localhost -U supatype_admin -d postgres \
  -c "grant supatype_privileged_role to app_admin;"

# After editing pg_guard.conf, reload. No restart needed.
psql -h localhost -U supatype_admin -d postgres \
  -c "select pg_reload_conf();"
```

### With Supatype

Every Supatype project runs on this image, with migrations, access rules, an API, a typed client and Studio generated from your TypeScript types. [Run it locally](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#local-dev) in a few commands. The full reference is the extension's [README](https://github.com/supatype/postgres/blob/develop/extensions/pg_guard/README.md).

## supatype_mask

Source: https://www.supatype.com/postgres/supatype-mask.html

Hide a column per row, not per table. supatype_mask masks reads and rejects writes on a single column, row by row. The rule is a SQL function you name in a security label, and the planner enforces it on every query.

### Why supatype_mask

Column privileges are all or nothing. Revoke SELECT on salary and a PostgREST request with no select list asks for every column, so the whole table answers 403 instead of a row with one field hidden. A view can put a CASE where the column was, but Postgres stores the view's column list when you create it. A column added later is invisible until someone re-runs CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW.

supatype_mask puts the rule on the column. You label it with a read predicate and a write predicate, and the planner rewrites every reference to that column into a CASE that calls your read predicate. That covers the select list, WHERE, ORDER BY, joins, subqueries, views, COPY TO and whole-row references such as to_jsonb(posts). A filter cannot be used to guess the hidden value.

Writes are judged per row too. If a client reads a masked null and sends the whole object back, the real value is kept. A caller who can see the value but may not change it gets a 42501 error. The rules are plain SQL functions, so the C extension stays small and the logic stays where you can read it.

### An example

`mask.sql`:

```sql
-- Readable by the post's author. Called once per row.
CREATE FUNCTION public.can_read_posts__salary(posts posts) RETURNS boolean
  LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$
    SELECT author_id = auth.uid() FROM (SELECT ($1).*) AS posts;
  $$;

-- Writable by HR. No arguments, so it runs once per scan.
CREATE FUNCTION public.can_write_posts__salary() RETURNS boolean
  LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$ SELECT auth.role() = 'hr' $$;

SECURITY LABEL FOR supatype ON COLUMN public.posts.salary
  IS 'MASK READ public.can_read_posts__salary WRITE public.can_write_posts__salary';

-- Every reference to posts.salary now plans as:
--   CASE WHEN public.can_read_posts__salary(posts)
--        THEN posts.salary ELSE NULL END
SELECT * FROM posts;                 -- other authors' salary is NULL
SELECT id FROM posts WHERE salary > 150;  -- filters on the masked value
SELECT sum(salary) FROM posts;       -- error if any row is unreadable
```

### supatype_mask or column GRANTs or a view per role

|  | column GRANTs or a view per role | supatype_mask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A request for every column | A column REVOKE makes PostgREST answer 403 for the whole table when no select list is given. | The column is returned, set to null on the rows the caller may not read. |
| Who can see the value | A GRANT decides per role, for every row in the table. | A predicate decides per row, for example author_id = auth.uid(). |
| Adding a column | A view stores a fixed column list, so a new column is missing until the view is recreated. | The label sits on the column and the table is queried directly. Nothing to recreate. |
| Clients the rule reaches | A view protects the queries that go through the view. | The rewrite happens in the planner, so psql, PostgREST and anything else on the database get the same answer. |
| Writing back a value you never saw | A view column built from CASE is read-only, so writes need a separate path and their own checks. | An unreadable value is kept. A readable value the caller may not change is rejected with an error. |
| Totals over hidden rows | sum() over a null-masking view adds up only the visible rows and says nothing. | sum(), max() and window aggregates are rejected per unreadable row, so a total is correct or an error. |
| Switching it off | Any role with the right privilege can GRANT the column back with one SQL statement. | No SQL statement disables masking for a role, a database or a session, not even as a superuser. It takes a config edit and a reload, or a restart. |

### What it does not do

- Postgres 17 or later only. The rewrite depends on planner internals that change between major versions.
- Logical replication is not filtered. WAL records are not query results, so a subscriber has to apply the same predicates itself.
- Roles in supatype_mask.exempt_roles and superusers see every column unmasked, by design.
- A non-leakproof operator applied to the predicate's own inputs can still reveal something through an error message. References to the masked column itself are safe.
- COPY FROM and MERGE are refused on a table with masked columns.
- A whole-row predicate runs once per row per masked column. On a full scan with a per-row lookup that can cost around 100 times the unmasked scan. A predicate with no arguments runs once per scan instead.
- An aggregate over a subquery that masked some rows skips those rows rather than raising an error.
- The library must be in shared_preload_libraries, which needs a restart. CREATE EXTENSION without the preload does nothing.
- A predicate declared IMMUTABLE, missing, or not returning boolean masks the column for everyone and logs a WARNING.

### Use it on its own

supatype_mask ships in the [supatype/postgres](https://www.supatype.com/postgres.html) image. Use the image as your Postgres, with or without the rest of Supatype.

```sh
# The image preloads supatype_mask and creates the extension on first boot.
docker run -d --name supatype-postgres \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your-password \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  supatype/postgres:17-latest

# Already set in the image's postgresql.conf:
#   shared_preload_libraries = '..., supatype_mask'
# and in /etc/postgresql-custom/supatype_mask.conf:
#   supatype_mask.exempt_roles = 'service_role,supatype_sql_editor'

# In any other database, create the extension yourself:
docker exec -it supatype-postgres psql -U supatype_admin -d mydb \
  -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS supatype_mask;"
```

### With Supatype

Every Supatype project runs on this image, with migrations, access rules, an API, a typed client and Studio generated from your TypeScript types. [Run it locally](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#local-dev) in a few commands. The full reference is the extension's [README](https://github.com/supatype/postgres/blob/develop/extensions/supatype_mask/README.md).

## CLI

Source: https://www.supatype.com/docs/cli.html

Every `supatype` command, grouped by what it is for. Descriptions are the ones `supatype --help` prints.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### Install and help

```sh
$ npm install -g @supatype/cli
$ supatype --help
$ supatype push --help
```

The npm package needs Node.js 22 or later. It is the install to use on Windows.

On a Linux or macOS machine without Node, such as a CI image or a server, install the standalone binary instead, with the script or with Homebrew:

```sh
$ curl -fsSL https://supatype.com/install.sh | bash
$ brew install supatype/tap/supatype
```

The script installs one binary to `~/.supatype/bin` and adds that directory to your shell profile. It checks the release signature with `openssl` before installing. Where `openssl` is missing or cannot check ed25519 signatures, as with the LibreSSL macOS ships, it says so and checks only the SHA256. On Alpine it installs the musl build, which needs `apk add libstdc++ libgcc`. The components `dev` downloads are built for glibc only, so run local stacks on a glibc image. `supatype self-update` updates a standalone install.

Run commands from the project directory, where `supatype.config.ts` is. Every command also takes `--project-name <name>`, which names the project for this run over `supatype.config.ts`. `supatype --version` prints the CLI version.

`--project-name` is the same as setting `SUPATYPE_PROJECT_NAME`, and it writes no file. The Compose project, the native database and the state directory under `~/.supatype/projects/` all follow it. Use it to run two stacks of one project side by side, each with its own `SUPATYPE_KONG_PORT`. The name may use lower case letters, digits, `-` and `_`, and must start with a letter or digit.

Many commands that reach a database take `--connection <url>` to override the config, and `--env <name>` to pick an environment when the project is linked.

> **CLOUD:** Commands marked **Cloud** need Supatype Cloud, which is coming soon. Everything else works locally and on a self-hosted stack.

### Project and local development

| Command | Description | Useful flags |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `init [name]` | Scaffold a new Supatype project | `-y, --defaults`, `--no-install`, `--no-keys`, `--admin-email`, `--admin-password`, `--no-admin` |
| `dev` | Start local Postgres, apply schema, and run supatype-server | `--no-watch`, `--stream`, `--port <port>`, `--reset-db` (Docker only), `--yes`, `--overwrite-drift` |
| `keys` | Generate ANON_KEY and SERVICE_ROLE_KEY JWTs from your JWT_SECRET | `--write`, `--force`, `--secret <secret>`, `--exp-years <years>` (default 10) |
| `status` | Show linked target status or local stack services | `--env <name>` |
| `logs` | Tail logs from the local stack | `--service <name>`, `--since <duration>` (default 5m), `-f, --follow` |
| `app add [dir]` | Configure app routing: `--static` for a built site, or proxy to a dev server | `--static`, `--port <port>` (default 3000), `--upstream <url>` |
| `app remove` | Set app.mode=none in supatype.config.ts |  |
| `admin create-user` | Create an admin user for the admin panel | `--email`, `--password` (asked for if left out), `--role` (default `admin`) |
| `admin set-role` | Change an existing user's admin role | `--email` and `--role`, both required |
| `admin list-users` | List users with Studio access | `--connection <url>` |
| `pg start` | Start Postgres for the current project | Native provider only |
| `pg stop` | Stop Postgres for the current project |  |
| `pg reset` | Stop Postgres, wipe the data directory, and re-initialise | `--force` |
| `pg psql [dbname]` | Open a psql shell connected to the project database |  |

`--role` is `admin`, `developer`, `editor` or `viewer`. See [Studio roles](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio-roles.html#grant). The first-run steps are in [Local development](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#local-dev).

`keys` prints the keys unless you pass `--write`, which fills blank keys in `.env`. Add `--force` to replace keys already there.

`dev` and `self-host compose up` refuse a `JWT_SECRET` shorter than 32 characters before starting anything, because the REST API cannot start with one. `init` generates a 64-character secret. To replace a short one, generate a longer secret (for example with `openssl rand -base64 48`), put it in `.env` as `JWT_SECRET`, then run `supatype keys --write --force` to sign new keys with it.

### Schema and database

| Command | Description | Useful flags |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `push` | Push schema to the database: diff, prompt for destructive changes, apply migration, generate types | `--yes`, `--connection <url>`, `--env <name>`, `--direct` (alias `--local`), `--overwrite-drift` |
| `diff` | Show planned schema changes without applying them (dry run) | `--connection <url>`, `--env <name>`, `--direct` |
| `generate` | Regenerate TypeScript types without running a migration |  |
| `migrate` | Write the SQL a push would apply, without applying it. Plain, it takes no lock your application waits on and the file records nothing: applied by hand, the next push finds the tables unmanaged. With `--record` the file also records the migration as a push does | `-o, --output <file>`, `--record`, `--force` |
| `migrations list` | List applied migrations with schema snapshot metadata | `--connection <url>`, `--env <name>` |
| `rollback` | Roll back the last applied migration | `--sync-schema`, `--no-sync-schema` |
| `reset` | Drop all managed tables and re-apply the schema from scratch (destructive) | `--yes`, `--connection <url>` |
| `rename [from] [to]` | Record a rename in supatype/renames.json, so every push applies it as a rename and keeps the data: `supatype rename member.name member.title`, or `supatype rename member members` for a table | `--prune` |
| `doctor` | Report schema drift between schema/index.ts and the live database | `--strict`, `--rebaseline`, `--accept-access-drift`, `--yes` |
| `adopt` | Hand Supatype the objects a push refuses because their names are taken; take objects back with `--release`, and hand them back with `--reclaim` | `--release <object...>`, `--reclaim <object...>`, `--key <object...>`, `--adopt-none`, `--yes` |
| `pull` | Scaffold schema/index.ts from live database introspection (draft, review before push) | `--connection <url>`, `--out <path>`, `--dry-run` |
| `introspect` | Introspect the live Postgres database (JSON or summary) | `--json`, `--out <path>` |
| `db check` | Check whether a database meets Supatype's requirements (for external Postgres) | `--connection <url>`, `--schema <name>`, `--emit`, `--fix`, `--authenticator-password <password>` |
| `types check` | Validate generated client augmentation wiring |  |

`--direct` skips the control plane of a linked project and runs the schema engine on this machine. `generate` reads only the schema, so it needs no database. `pull` prints its draft unless you pass `--out`. `migrations list` shows each migration's author, how many schema files its snapshot holds and their compressed size, and the renames it applied.

A push never guesses a rename. A column that disappears while a new one appears is a drop and an add, and the drop loses data. In a terminal the push asks whether you meant a rename and records a yes in `supatype/renames.json`. Anywhere else it refuses and prints the `supatype rename` command that records it.

An object passed to `adopt` is named as `doctor` names it: `kind:table.name`, or `kind:name` for a table. Studio shows the result under [Schema objects](https://www.supatype.com/docs/studio.html#database).

> **PULL:** `pull` writes a draft. Review it before you push: it types every uuid `id` column as `SupatypeAuthUserId` and does not write `tableName`, so fix those by hand.

### Data and seeds

| Command | Description | Useful flags |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `seed [file]` | Run database seeds: optional single file; else all seeds/*.ts (alphabetical); else seed.ts | `--status`, `--atomic`, `--connection <dsn>`, `--environment <name>` |
| `cache rest list` | List cached REST GET entries | `--table <name>`, `--json` |
| `cache rest get <key>` | Show one cache entry (full key) | `--json` |
| `cache rest delete <key>` | Delete one cache entry |  |
| `cache rest flush` | Flush REST cache entries | `--table <name>`, `--yes` |

`seed` refuses to run against a project linked to Supatype Cloud unless you pass `--force`. See [Seeding](https://www.supatype.com/docs/seeding.html).

### Functions and hooks

| Command | Description | Useful flags |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `functions new <name>` | Scaffold a new edge function |  |
| `functions serve` | Start a local Deno server that serves all functions with hot reload | `--port <port>` (default 54321), `--env-file <path>` (default `.env.local`) |
| `functions invoke <name>` | Invoke a local or deployed function | `--data <json>`, `--auth`, `--local` |
| `functions deploy` | Deploy all functions (or `--only <name>` for one) to the linked project | `--only <name>`, `--env <name>`, `--dry-run` |
| `functions list` **Cloud** | List all deployed functions for the linked project |  |
| `functions delete <name>` **Cloud** | Remove a deployed function |  |
| `functions logs <name>` **Cloud** | Tail logs for a deployed function | `--since <duration>` (default 1h) |
| `functions env list`, `set <KEY=value>`, `unset <key>` **Cloud** | Manage function environment variables |  |
| `hooks new <name>` | Scaffold a hook handler |  |
| `hooks list` | Show the hooks the schema declares and whether each one can run |  |

On an unlinked project with a self-hosted Compose stack, `functions deploy` uploads nothing: the worker serves `functions/` from disk, so it lists the functions and prints the command that restarts the worker. Otherwise it deploys to the linked project, or to Supatype Cloud. On a self-hosted stack, read function logs in Studio. See [Functions](https://www.supatype.com/docs/functions.html).

### Self-host and deploy

| Command | Description | Useful flags |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `self-host compose render` | Render deterministic self-host compose artifacts |  |
| `self-host compose up` | Render and start compose services | `-d, --detach` (on by default) |
| `self-host compose down` | Stop compose services (volumes are kept unless `--volumes`) | `--volumes`, `-y, --yes` |
| `self-host compose restart <service>` | Recreate one service with the current config and .env, leaving the others running |  |
| `self-host compose status` | Show compose service status |  |
| `self-host compose logs` | Tail compose logs | `--service <name>`, `-f, --follow` |
| `add domain [domain]` | Add a custom domain with automatic HTTPS (self-host) | `--email <email>` for Let's Encrypt |
| `link` | Link this project to cloud or self-host (unified .supatype/link.json) | `--url <url>`, `--token <token>`, `--env <name>`, `--fix-gitignore` |
| `envs list` | List linked environments |  |
| `envs use <name>` | Set the default environment |  |
| `deploy` | Deploy schema and app, Supatype Cloud by default when linked (`supatype link`); pass `--local` for engine + your database | `--env <name>` (default `production`), `--schema-only`, `--app-only`, `--skip-build`, `--preview`, `--yes`, `--overwrite-drift` |
| `deploy rollback` | Roll back to the previous static site deployment | `--to <id>`, `--env <name>` |
| `deploy status` | Show current deployment status | `--env <name>` |
| `deploy logs [version]` | Show build logs for a deployment | `--env <name>` |

Every `self-host compose` command renders `.supatype/self-host/docker-compose.yml` again before it runs. The file names each bind mount by its absolute path on this machine, and names its Compose project `supatype-` plus `project.name`. So `docker compose -f .supatype/self-host/docker-compose.yml` run by hand reaches the same stack, and a project moved to another folder is picked up by the next command.

A render keeps the stack in the mode it runs in. While `supatype dev` runs for the project, commands such as `push`, `update` and `self-host compose` render dev mode. Otherwise they use the mode of the running `server` container, and standalone when none is running. So a push to a production stack leaves it standalone.

For a self-hosted stack, `link --url` takes the stack's gateway URL and `--token` its `SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`. The full walkthrough is in [Self-host](https://www.supatype.com/docs/#self-host) and [Deploy to a VM with GitHub Actions](https://www.supatype.com/deploy-vm-github-actions.html).

### Supatype Cloud

All of these need Supatype Cloud, which is coming soon.

| Command | Description | Useful flags |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `login` | Sign in to Supatype Cloud (stores refreshable session for push/deploy) | `--email <email>`, `--password <password>` (prefer `SUPATYPE_PASSWORD`) |
| `logout` | Clear stored Supatype Cloud credentials |  |
| `whoami` | Show the current Supatype Cloud session |  |
| `link --project <slug>` | Link this project to cloud or self-host (unified .supatype/link.json) | `--token <token>`, `--env <name>` |
| `projects list` | List all projects in your organisation |  |
| `projects create <name>` | Create a new project | `--tier <tier>`, `--region <region>` |
| `projects pause <slug>` | Pause a project |  |
| `projects resume <slug>` | Resume a paused project |  |
| `domains list`, `add <domain>`, `remove <domainId>`, `verify <domainId>` | Manage custom domains for a project |  |
| `envs create <name>` | Create a cloud environment (staging/preview) |  |
| `db connection-string` | Show the database connection string for the linked project | `--transaction`, `--env <name>` |
| `db reset-password` | Reset the database password for the linked project | `--env <name>` |

### Binaries and updates

| Command | Description | Useful flags |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `self-update` | Update the supatype CLI (npm or standalone CDN binary) | `--force` |
| `update` | Download the latest component binaries and update versions in supatype.config.ts | `--check` |
| `engine status` | Run the host engine binary's `--version` and show which binary answered |  |
| `cache list` | List cached component binaries and their sizes | `--project <path>` |
| `cache clean [component] [version]` | Remove cached binaries not pinned by local project configs | `--dry-run`, `--force`, `--project <path>` |
| `migrate-from-v1` | Codemod runtime model() schema DSL into RFC v2 Model<> type aliases | `--schema <path>`, `--write` |

Binaries are cached in `~/.supatype/cache/`. `cache clean --force` removes every cached binary, pinned or not.

## Licensing

Source: https://www.supatype.com/licensing.html

What you can do with Supatype, in plain words. This page is a guide and is not legal advice. It does not change any licence: where it and a licence differ, the licence governs.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

### In one minute

**SDKs** (MIT): The client SDKs, framework bindings and plugins. Use them for anything.

**CLI and services** (APACHE 2.0): The CLI, Studio and the services (storage, realtime, functions worker). Use them for anything.

**Schema engine** (BSL 1.1): Source-available under the Business Source License 1.1 (SPDX `BUSL-1.1`), and its source is at [github.com/supatype/schema-engine](https://github.com/supatype/schema-engine). You can read it, change it, redistribute it and run it in production.

- The one thing you cannot do without a commercial licence: offer Supatype or the engine to others as a hosted or managed service, paid or free, or sell a product whose primary value is the engine.
- Each engine version becomes **Apache 2.0** on its Change Date, four years after that version's release.

The engine's licence, with its Additional Use Grant, is in the `LICENSE` file at the root of the [engine's repository](https://github.com/supatype/schema-engine) and ships with every engine release, beside the binary on `releases.supatype.com` and at `/LICENSE` in the `supatype/schema-engine` image. `supatype-engine licence` prints the exact terms for the version you have.

### Can I? Yes

| Can I... | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Build and sell my own app on Supatype? | Yes, commercial apps included. That is what the engine is for. |
| Self-host Supatype for my company? | Yes, on infrastructure you own, rent or control, for your own applications and products. |
| Run it for my clients as an agency? | Yes. You can build, host and maintain applications for clients, including one Supatype stack per client's app. |
| Let my app's users define their own fields? | Yes, where that schema management is incidental to what your app does (custom fields in a CRM, for example). |
| Modify the engine and use it internally? | Yes. Your changes stay under BSL 1.1. |
| Fork it? | Yes. A fork carries the same licence and the same limits. |
| Use it in a free open source project? | Yes, as long as the project is not itself a hosted Supatype-style service for others. |
| Use it inside a group of companies? | Yes. Affiliates under common control count as you, so an internal platform team can serve the whole group. |

### Can I? Not without a commercial licence

- **Run a hosted Supatype, or a Supatype-compatible backend, for others.** Paid or free. The licence calls this a Competing Service: a hosted or managed database, backend or schema management service where third parties define, migrate or manage their own schemas, or build their own applications.
- **Sell a product whose primary value is the engine.** For example, a schema migration or database change management tool built on it, or a backend platform that includes it. The licence calls this a Competing Product.

If your product is not competing when you first make it generally available, it does not become competing later because Supatype ships a new version or a new product.

> **FREE HOSTING COUNTS:** Some source-available licences only restrict paid offerings. Ours restricts free hosted offerings too, because a free hosted Supatype competes with Supatype Cloud just as much.

### Grey areas, worked through

| Situation | Allowed? |
| --- | --- |
| A SaaS where each customer adds custom fields to their records | Yes. Field management is incidental to the product. |
| An internal platform team running Supatype for many teams in the same company or group | Yes. That is internal use by affiliates under common control. |
| An agency hosting several clients' apps, each on its own Supatype stack | Yes. |
| An agency offering clients a general platform on which they build their own apps | No, that is a Competing Service. |
| A hosting company offering one-click Supatype for its customers | Needs a commercial licence. |
| A hosted app builder whose customers design their own databases | Needs a commercial licence. |

Not sure where you fall? Ask at [licensing@supatype.com](mailto:licensing@supatype.com).

### Versions and dates

- **Each version has its own Change Date**, set when it is released, to the release date plus four years. It is written in that version's `LICENSE`.
- **On the Change Date** that version, and only that version, becomes available under the Apache License 2.0. Later versions keep their own dates.
- **Commits between releases** on the engine's `main` branch are part of the next release and take its Change Date.
- **All earlier versions and commits** are made available under the same BSL 1.1 terms, with the same Additional Use Grant and the same Change Date as 0.7.0. That includes 0.1.5 to 0.6.0, which were distributed as binaries without a licence, and commits from before the engine's repository had a `LICENSE` file.

### The other packages

| Component | Licence |
| --- | --- |
| `client`, `types`, `react`, `react-native`, `vue`, `svelte`, `solid`, `ssr`, the auth UI packages, the plugin packages, `ui`, `common` | MIT |
| CLI, Studio, storage, realtime, functions worker, self-host control plane, and the rest of the `supatype/supatype` repository | Apache 2.0 |
| Schema engine (`supatype-engine`, image `supatype/schema-engine`) | BSL 1.1, Apache 2.0 on each version's Change Date |

The CLI downloads the engine as a separate binary; the CLI's own licence is unaffected. Your application code, schemas and data are yours, whatever you build them with.

### Contributing

Contributions need a signed [Contributor License Agreement](https://github.com/supatype/supatype/blob/main/CLA.md), signed once through CLA Assistant on your first pull request. It is a licence, not an assignment: you keep the copyright and grant Supatype Ltd the right to use and relicense your contribution, which is what lets each version move to Apache 2.0 and be offered under commercial terms. Contributing gives you no extra rights in the product, and takes none away.

### Commercial licences

To run a hosted service on the engine, embed it in a product you sell, or anything else the grant does not cover, contact [licensing@supatype.com](mailto:licensing@supatype.com). The Licensor is Supatype Ltd.

### Why BSL

We want you to be able to read the code that changes your database, run it wherever you like, and never depend on us to keep your app alive. We also need a business that can pay for the engine. The BSL lets us give you the first without a hosting company taking the engine and competing with Supatype Cloud on day one. Every version still becomes Apache 2.0 after four years.

## Changelog

Source: https://www.supatype.com/changelog.html

What changed in each Supatype release, in short. Every pull request is listed on [GitHub releases](https://github.com/supatype/supatype/releases).

### 0.7.0

27 October 2026

- **Supatype knows what it owns.** `supatype adopt` takes over a table a push refused, `--release` hands it back, and `--reclaim` takes a released one again. Studio has a Schema objects view of all of it.
- **`supatype doctor`** shows drifted, conflicting and released objects, and `--rebaseline` starts the record afresh.
- **Safer pushes.** A push asks before it puts back access changed outside Supatype, and offers to declare a rename before it asks to drop data. A change that rewrites a whole table needs your consent.
- **Realtime** delivers deletes with the old row, judged by the same read rules as everything else.
- **Auth providers** are set with `auth.providers` in the config.
- **Studio** gains a Realtime Inspector for self-hosted stacks.
- Secrets and the database URL no longer appear on any child process's command line.

### 0.3

23 September to 2 October 2026

- **Publishing, drafts and versions** for content models.
- **Functions** run concurrently, with their logs.
- **Storage** moves to SeaweedFS.
- **Model caches.** A model can declare a cache, and a push refuses one that cannot be served.
- **Vue, Svelte and Solid** reach parity with React.
- A model can set its own Studio labels (0.3.6).

### 0.2

2 to 3 September 2026

- **Supatype's own auth** replaces GoTrue in the CLI, the client and Studio.
- A push refuses a schema that the database engine in use cannot enforce.

### Earlier

Releases before 0.2 are on [GitHub releases](https://github.com/supatype/supatype/releases).
